schema.name: Purpose
schema.Description: Host a catalog of independent Effortless projects (rulebook-examples/<project>/), each a self-contained rulebook that fully captures one domain and selects the subset of platform substrates it needs. data.Name: Rulebook is the IR
data.Statement: The rulebook JSON is the portable intermediate representation. Every other artifact is mechanically derivable from it.
data.Why: If any artifact is hand-edited authoritatively, conformance no longer follows from a single source. The 'all substrates compute identically' claim depends on one IR.
data.Implication: Generated files are disposable; the rulebook JSON is the only file that is sacred.

data.Name: No privileged substrate
data.Statement: Postgres, Airtable, Excel, Python, Go, OWL, COBOL — every substrate is a peer projection of the rulebook. None is the reference.
data.Why: Privileging one substrate quietly redefines 'correct' as 'matches that substrate' instead of 'matches the rulebook', which is the actual SSoT.
data.Implication: Substrate properties (maturity, transpiler source, expressive completeness) are facts about implementations, not authority rankings.

data.Name: SSoT is locally designated
data.Statement: The 'answer key' for a conformance run is whichever substrate the user designates as SSoT for that run — Airtable export, Excel workbook, hand-edited JSON, or a Postgres dump.
data.Why: If the answer key is fixed, the methodology only works in one deployment mode. Locality lets the same harness validate Airtable-driven, Excel-driven, or JSON-driven projects.
data.Implication: Conformance reports must name the chosen SSoT for the run; trustworthy substrates witness, they do not crown.

data.Name: Hub-and-spoke topology
data.Statement: The rulebook is the hub. Input spokes (Airtable, LLM, admin portal, hand edits) write to it. Output spokes (substrates) read from it. Spokes never talk to each other.
data.Why: Direct spoke-to-spoke traffic re-introduces the n×n integration problem the rulebook was created to eliminate.
data.Implication: If you find yourself wiring a substrate to consume another substrate's output, you are violating the topology — route through the rulebook.

data.Name: Fail loudly, never fall back
data.Statement: When a file or value is not where it is expected, the code fails with the exact expected path. It does not check a second location, default to a guess, or return an empty object with a warning.
data.Why: Silent fallbacks mask the bug they are working around and cause 100% conformance against the wrong data.
data.Implication: Defaults derived from the SSoT are fine. Defaults that substitute a guess are not.

data.Name: Project rulebook ≠ demo rulebook
data.Statement: The platform rulebook (this file) is the parent describing ERB itself. Demo rulebooks under rulebook-examples/ are children describing one business domain each. They never mix.
data.Why: Mixing platform-meta with business-data couples the wrapper to a domain, which destroys the wrapper's portability.
data.Implication: Portal config tables (AppUsers, AppNavigation, etc.) live ONLY in this file. Business tables (Customers, Episodes, etc.) live ONLY in their demo rulebook.

data.Name: Admin portal ≠ a domain
data.Statement: The admin portal is the app; a domain is a document the app opens. Their databases are separate (erb_admin_portal vs erb_<domain>) and the names never merge.
data.Why: Names like erb_admin_<domain> conflate the editor with the thing being edited, which leads to drift between portal state and document state.
data.Implication: Two Postgres connections at all times: one to the portal's own DB, one to the active document's DB.

data.Name: Build = generate + test + report
data.Statement: Every build runs all transpilers, then runs every substrate's conformance test, then regenerates and opens the report.
data.Why: A build that skips the test step produces output of unknown correctness; the methodology's value is the conformance proof, not the codegen.
data.Implication: There is no 'build without testing' menu option. If a substrate has no take-test.sh, that is a bug to fix, not a case to handle.

data.Name: Portal/CLI parity
data.Statement: The admin portal and ./start.sh --cli are peer interfaces to the same effortless.json pipeline. Every portal mutation shells out to the same `effortless` CLI command.
data.Why: Two divergent implementations of 'install a tool' or 'run a build' will drift; conformance claims become qualified ('works in CLI, fails in portal').
data.Implication: If the portal grows logic the CLI does not have, that logic moves into the CLI and the portal calls it.

data.Name: Write-through invariant
data.Statement: The portal's editor Postgres DB is live; the rulebook JSON is durable. Every save writes to BOTH in the same logical transaction.
data.Why: If Postgres ever wins alone, JSON drifts and the SSoT property is violated. If JSON ever wins alone, the live editor lies about state.
data.Implication: Drop Postgres at any time and rebuild from JSON; never the other direction.

data.Name: Rulebook is a complete spec
data.Statement: A rulebook alone — no accompanying source code, no documentation — is sufficient for any frontier LLM to answer any question about the domain or produce a faithful implementation of the rules in any language, platform, or context.
data.Why: This is the load-bearing portability claim. If the rulebook is not self-sufficient, the methodology degrades into documentation-plus-code where the docs lie and the code is the real spec.
data.Implication: Anything required to understand or reproduce the domain MUST live in the rulebook. If a generated artifact contains business logic not derivable from the rulebook, that logic belongs IN the rulebook, not in the substrate.

data.Name: Build is convergent, not additive
data.Statement: `effortless build` makes downstream artifacts conform to the current rulebook: additions appear, removals disappear, renames propagate. Generated artifacts are a projection of the rulebook's current state, never an accumulation of past states.
data.Why: This is the property that distinguishes ERB from a conventional code generator. Codegen accumulates (you run it, code appears, removing things from the spec doesn't remove the corresponding code). ERB conforms — the projection is total, so the rulebook stays the single source of truth in both directions.
data.Implication: Hand-edits to generated artifacts are erased on the next build by design. The rulebook is the only place to add, modify, OR remove behavior.

data.Name: Formula dialect is a rulebook property
data.ShortName: Formula dialect is a rulebook property
data.Statement: A rulebook declares which formula dialect it uses (Excel, Airtable, …). Substrates implement the dialect's semantics; the conformance proof is 'all substrates compute identically under this rulebook's declared dialect.' The dialect is metadata on the rulebook, not a property of ERB.
data.Why: Hardcoding one dialect as 'the ERB formula language' would couple the methodology to that dialect's quirks and exclude domains that already think in another (e.g. Airtable-native teams). The conformance machinery doesn't care which dialect is in use; it only cares that every substrate's transpiler implements the same one.
data.Implication: Excel is the current default because domain experts can read it, but it is not invariant. A rulebook may declare a different dialect, and substrate transpilers must honor the declared dialect.

data.Name: Postgres is the reference substrate
data.WrongFraming: Postgres is the reference substrate with no expressive gaps; other substrates are demonstrations with gaps relative to it.
data.CorrectFraming: Postgres is one of N peer substrates. It happens to have few expressive gaps in practice, which makes it a convenient witness — but witnessing is not the same as crowning.
data.Why: Calling Postgres 'the reference' redefines 'correct' as 'matches Postgres'. The actual SSoT is the rulebook (or the user-designated answer-key substrate for that run). Postgres being trustworthy doesn't make it privileged.
data.ExampleContext: Said by Claude when describing the repo on 2026-05-25. Caught by user in the same turn.

data.Name: The rulebook JSON is always the SSoT
data.WrongFraming: The rulebook JSON file is the single source of truth in every deployment.
data.CorrectFraming: The rulebook is the portable IR. The SSoT for a given conformance run is whichever spoke the user designates — Airtable export, Excel workbook, hand-edited JSON, etc. If Airtable is the SSoT, the rulebook JSON is downstream from it.
data.Why: Treating the JSON as universally authoritative ignores that input spokes can BE the SSoT. The framework supports several deployment modes; only one of them has the JSON as primary.
data.ExampleContext: Implicit in any phrasing like 'the JSON is the SSoT, period' without naming the deployment mode.

data.Name: IsProduction = trustworthy
data.WrongFraming: Substrates with IsProduction=true (Postgres, Excel, Entity Framework) are the trustworthy ones; the others are proof-of-concept.
data.CorrectFraming: 'Production' here means 'backed by an officially-licensed transpiler' — a fact about who built the generator, not about whether the substrate computes correctly. Trustworthiness is measured by passing the conformance tests.
data.Why: Using one column to mean both 'authorized vendor built it' AND 'we trust its output' conflates provenance with correctness. They are independent properties; conformance is what proves correctness.
data.ExampleContext: The original ExecutionSubstrates.IsProduction column collapses these two meanings.

data.Name: Project rulebook is a demo rulebook
data.WrongFraming: Portal-config tables (UserRoles, AppUsers, AppNavigation) belong in whichever rulebook is active.
data.CorrectFraming: Portal-config tables live ONLY in the project rulebook (this file). Demo rulebooks contain only their domain's business tables. Two file reads, two concerns, never merged.
data.Why: Mixing platform-meta with business-data couples the wrapper to one domain. The wrapper has to work for every demo; the demo has to travel without portal config.
data.ExampleContext: Anytime someone proposes 'just add UserRoles to acme-llc-rulebook.json so the portal works against it'.

data.Name: Admin portal is named after a domain
data.WrongFraming: Database names like erb_admin_acme_llc, erb_admin_star_trek — admin portal plus the active domain.
data.CorrectFraming: erb_admin_portal (singular) for the portal's own state; erb_<domain> for each document. The word 'admin' appears only in the portal's own DB name and never with a domain suffix.
data.Why: The naming itself proves the category error: the app is not named after the document it opens. Word's install directory is not 'Word_my_resume'.
data.ExampleContext: If you see erb_admin_<domain> in code, the code is wrong — flag it as a category-error bug, not as fact.

data.Name: Silent fallback when a path is missing
data.WrongFraming: If a rulebook file is not at the expected path, check a legacy location or return {} with a warning.
data.CorrectFraming: Fail loudly with the exact expected path. Every fallback hides a bug; there are no compatibility shims in a project this young.
data.Why: Fallbacks make conformance run against the wrong data and report 100% pass, masking the real failure. A loud failure produces a fixable stack trace.
data.ExampleContext: Any `if not os.path.exists` followed by a default that isn't derived from the SSoT.

data.Name: Defaults are fallbacks
data.WrongFraming: All `or`-defaults are fallbacks and should be removed.
data.CorrectFraming: A default computed from the SSoT (e.g. `or f"erb_{active_domain}"`) is NOT a fallback — it's the deterministically-correct value the env var would override. A fallback is one that silently substitutes a guess.
data.Why: Over-correcting on the 'no fallbacks' rule removes correct SSoT-derived defaults and forces every caller to set env vars. The test: if the default would still be correct after the env var was unset by accident, it's a default.
data.ExampleContext: DATABASE_URL with a default of `erb_{active_domain}` is fine. DATABASE_URL with a default of `postgres` is a bug.

data.Name: Build can run without testing
data.WrongFraming: Add a 'build without testing' option so users can iterate faster.
data.CorrectFraming: Build = generate + test + regenerate report + open. The conformance proof is the point of the build; codegen alone produces output of unknown correctness.
data.Why: Splitting build from test makes 'did this work' ambiguous and silently allows substrates to drift apart between formal runs.
data.ExampleContext: Any menu addition like '[B] Build only' or '[R] Regenerate report only'.

data.Name: Portal grows logic the CLI lacks
data.WrongFraming: It's easier to implement 'install a tool' directly in the portal backend than to call the effortless CLI.
data.CorrectFraming: The portal shells out to the same `effortless` CLI command the user would run by hand. Both surfaces are peer interfaces to the same pipeline.
data.Why: Two implementations of the same operation will drift; conformance claims become qualified by interface.
data.ExampleContext: Anywhere the portal backend reaches into effortless.json directly instead of invoking `effortless -install`.

data.Name: Postgres editor wins over JSON
data.WrongFraming: Persist edits to Postgres now and write them to JSON on demand (lazy sync).
data.CorrectFraming: Every save is write-through: Postgres and JSON in the same logical transaction. Postgres is the live editor; JSON is the durable SSoT.
data.Why: Lazy sync means a crash leaves the JSON behind the editor — and the JSON is the only file that travels with the repo.
data.ExampleContext: Anywhere a PATCH endpoint touches the DB but defers writing JSON.

data.Name: Swappable active domain
data.WrongFraming: The platform has one stack and a 'swappable active domain' — switch the active domain (acme-llc, star-trek, talisman-advanced, …) and the entire stack regenerates against it.
data.CorrectFraming: rulebook-examples/ is a CATALOG of N independent Effortless projects. Each project owns its own rulebook and picks the subset of the platform's 15+ substrates it needs (acme-llc uses all 15+; most use 3+). active-domain.txt is a convenience pointer for the orchestrator/portal — not the architecture.
data.Why: The 'swappable' framing implies one shared stack parameterized by domain. In reality each project is self-contained; the platform is a catalog, not a runtime that mounts one domain at a time. Calling them 'swappable' hides the fact that projects choose different substrate subsets and evolve independently.
data.ExampleContext: README phrasing like 'Swappable demo domains — switch the active domain and the entire stack regenerates against it.' Caught by user 2026-05-25.

data.Name: ERB is a code generator
data.WrongFraming: ERB generates code from a declarative spec — like any other code generator.
data.CorrectFraming: `effortless build` is CONVERGENT, not additive. Downstream artifacts mirror the current rulebook: additions appear, removals disappear, renames propagate. A conventional code generator only adds; ERB conforms. The rulebook is the SSoT in BOTH directions.
data.Why: Calling ERB a 'code generator' anchors readers on a category (one-way emit-and-forget) that misses the load-bearing property. The convergence is what lets the rulebook stay authoritative — if removals didn't propagate, generated code would silently outlive its spec and the SSoT claim would collapse.
data.ExampleContext: Any framing like 'multi-substrate code generation from declarative rulebooks' without the convergence property called out.

data.Name: Excel formulas are the formula language of ERB
data.WrongFraming: ERB formulas are Excel-compatible (IF, AND, OR, CONCAT, LEFT, RIGHT, …) — that's how calculated fields work in ERB.
data.CorrectFraming: ERB rulebooks declare a formula DIALECT. Excel is the current default because domain experts can read it, but Airtable dialect (or any other) is equally valid. The dialect is a per-rulebook property; the conformance claim is 'all substrates compute identically UNDER THIS RULEBOOK'S DECLARED DIALECT.'
data.Why: Hardcoding Excel as 'the ERB formula language' couples the methodology to one dialect's quirks (1-indexed strings, specific function set, etc.) and excludes teams who already think in another dialect. The dialect is metadata on the rulebook; the platform's job is to make every substrate's transpiler honor whichever dialect is declared.
data.ExampleContext: CLAUDE.md 'Key Principles' listing 'Formula semantics are Excel-compatible' as a property of ERB, or any rulebook doc that names Excel functions as if they were the language rather than the dialect.
data.AxiomShortName: Formula dialect is a rulebook property

PlatformFeatures.Description: The catalog of distinctive features the ERB platform offers. The rulebook is the formal SSoT for this list; the repo's README and per-feature README files MUST conform to these rows. Each feature has a one-line summary (the elevator pitch), a Tier (headline vs additional), a Priority (sort order within tier), and a ReadmeFilePath (where the long-form explanation lives — even if it's still a stub). IsReadmeStub is calculated so 'which READMEs are still missing' is a queryable fact, not a tribal one. Many features reference an OntologyAxiom — that's the axiom the feature operationalizes.

data.Name: Abstract Derivative Percentage (ADP)
data.OneLineSummary: A first-class, measurable percentage of any ERB project that is derivative (mechanically rebuildable) vs. hand-written — `effortless -clean` deletes everything derivative, build restores it, and the LOC delta is the ADP.
data.ReadmeStubContent: ADP draws a bright red line between Derivative Code (rebuildable on demand) and Hand Code (would be permanently lost without backup). Measured as (LOC_before_cleanall - LOC_after_cleanall) / LOC_before_cleanall. A pure scaffold starts at ~100%; a typical ERB project lands at 60-80%.

data.Name: effortless -clean / implicit clean before build
data.OneLineSummary: `effortless -clean` removes every file whose OverwriteMode is ALWAYS, plus every NEVER-mode file that still matches the original generator output — both are Derivative Code by definition. Every build runs this implicitly first, so 'following along' is the default.
data.ReadmeStubContent: Clean is the mechanism that lets ADP be measured. OverwriteMode=ALWAYS files are always derivative; OverwriteMode=NEVER files are derivative as long as their content still matches the generator output. Once a NEVER file is customized, it crosses into Hand Code and clean leaves it alone.

data.Name: Rulebook as IR / Hub-and-Spoke Topology
data.OneLineSummary: The rulebook JSON is the hub; every input (Airtable, LLM, admin portal, hand edits) and every output (Postgres, Python, Go, Excel, OWL, …) is a spoke. Spokes never talk to each other — they all route through the rulebook, eliminating the n×n integration problem.
data.ReadmeStubContent: The topology IS the architecture: one durable IR, N peer spokes. Generated artifacts are projections of the rulebook, never accumulations.

data.Name: Convergent Builds (not Additive Codegen)
data.OneLineSummary: `effortless build` makes downstream artifacts mirror the current rulebook — additions appear, removals disappear, renames propagate. A conventional code generator only adds; ERB conforms, in both directions.
data.ReadmeStubContent: Conventional codegen is one-way: you remove a field from the spec, the generated column lingers until someone notices. ERB is two-way: removing a field from the rulebook removes it from every substrate on the next build. This is what makes the rulebook stay authoritative.

data.Name: No Privileged Substrate / Portability
data.OneLineSummary: Every substrate (Postgres, Python, Go, OWL, COBOL, Excel, English, ARM64) is a peer projection of the rulebook. Languages not yet invented can be plugged in down the road by writing one transpiler — the rest of the stack lights up unchanged.
data.ReadmeStubContent: No substrate is the reference. Trustworthiness is measured by passing the conformance tests, not by being Postgres. This is what justifies 'portable across not-yet-invented languages'.

data.Name: Conformance Testing Across Substrates
data.OneLineSummary: Every build runs every substrate's conformance test against a locally-designated answer key and shows the pass/fail matrix. Substrate agreement is the empirical receipt that the rulebook is the SSoT.
data.ReadmeStubContent: There is no 'build without testing'. Build = generate + test + regenerate report + open. If a substrate has no take-test, that is a bug to fix, not a case to handle.

data.Name: Locally-Designated SSoT
data.OneLineSummary: The 'answer key' for a conformance run is whichever spoke the user designates — Airtable export, Excel workbook, hand-edited JSON, Postgres dump. The same harness validates Airtable-driven, Excel-driven, and JSON-driven projects.
data.ReadmeStubContent: SSoT is a per-run designation, not a global property. The rulebook is the portable IR; the SSoT for a given run is whichever substrate the user nominates as the oracle.

data.Name: Portal/CLI Parity
data.OneLineSummary: The admin portal and `./start.sh --cli` are peer interfaces to the same `effortless.json` pipeline. Every portal mutation shells out to the same `effortless` CLI command, so the two surfaces cannot drift.
data.ReadmeStubContent: Two surfaces, one pipeline. If the portal grows logic the CLI doesn't have, that logic moves into the CLI and the portal calls it.

data.Name: Write-Through Invariant
data.OneLineSummary: The portal's editor Postgres DB is live; the rulebook JSON is durable. Every save writes to BOTH in the same logical transaction — drop Postgres at any time and rebuild from JSON, never the other direction.
data.ReadmeStubContent: The rulebook JSON is the only file that travels with the repo. Postgres is convenience; JSON is truth. Lazy sync is forbidden.

data.Name: Fail Loudly, Never Fall Back
data.OneLineSummary: When a file or value isn't where it's expected, the code fails with the exact expected path. No silent fallbacks. Defaults derived from the SSoT are fine; defaults that substitute a guess are not.
data.ReadmeStubContent: Silent fallbacks make conformance run against the wrong data and report 100% pass, masking the real failure. A loud failure produces a fixable stack trace.

data.Name: Rulebook Is a Complete Spec
data.OneLineSummary: A rulebook alone — no accompanying source code, no documentation — is sufficient for any frontier LLM to answer any question about the domain or produce a faithful implementation in any language.
data.ReadmeStubContent: The load-bearing portability claim. If the rulebook were not self-sufficient, the methodology would degrade into docs-plus-code where the docs lie and the code is the real spec.

data.Name: Per-Rulebook Formula Dialect
data.OneLineSummary: Each rulebook declares its formula dialect (Excel, Airtable, …). Substrates honor the declared dialect; the conformance claim is 'all substrates compute identically under THIS rulebook's declared dialect.'
data.ReadmeStubContent: Excel is the current default because domain experts can read it, but it is not invariant. Dialect is metadata on the rulebook, not a property of ERB.
data.AxiomShortName: Formula dialect is a rulebook property

data.Name: Project Rulebook ≠ Demo Rulebook
data.OneLineSummary: The platform rulebook describes ERB itself; the demo rulebooks under `rulebook-examples/` describe one business domain each. They never mix — portal config lives only in the platform rulebook; business tables live only in their demo rulebook.
data.ReadmeStubContent: Mixing platform-meta with business-data couples the wrapper to a domain, which destroys portability. Two file reads, two concerns, never merged.

data.Name: Admin Portal ≠ a Domain
data.OneLineSummary: The portal is the app (`erb_admin_portal` DB); a domain is a document the app opens (`erb_<domain>` DB). The name 'admin' never appears with a domain suffix — `erb_admin_<domain>` is a category-error red flag.
data.ReadmeStubContent: Word's install directory isn't named after any document; a .docx isn't named after Word. Two connections, two purposes, two categories.

data.Name: Local Transpiler Host
data.OneLineSummary: The effortless CLI hosts this repo's own transpilers on `127.0.0.1:4242`, so repo-local transpilers and officially-licensed ones look identical to a build.
data.ReadmeStubContent: Each tool is a folder under `effortless-tools/<name>/` whose transpiler.py calls orchestration/local_tool_shim.py; the shim hands the injector the rulebook the CLI delivered. `effortless serve -port 4242` keeps one host resident.

data.Name: Self-Hosting Platform (dog-fooding)
data.OneLineSummary: The orchestration tool, the React explorer, and the local transpiler host are themselves generated from the governing rulebook in `effortless-rulebook/effortless-rulebook.json` — ERB is its own first customer.
data.ReadmeStubContent: The wrapper eats its own dog food. Every feature, screen, API, and table you see in the portal exists because the platform rulebook says it does.

data.Name: Skills as LLM force multiplier
data.OneLineSummary: The rulebook gives the LLM something to operate on; the skills give it the instructions for how to operate — together they replace a learning curve that previously cost weeks.
data.ReadmeStubContent: Before ERB, every developer had to teach their LLM the ERB conventions from scratch. Skills pre-encode that learning — naming rules, pipeline mechanics, formula semantics, the Effortless loop — so the LLM arrives already trained. The rulebook is the subject matter; the skills are the curriculum. Without the rulebook there is nothing for the skills to operate on. Without the skills the LLM has to rediscover the conventions by trial and error.

RulebookDomains.Description: Customer ontologies: each domain has its own rulebook + substrate generation. Domains form a TREE — ParentDomainId links a more-elaborate domain back to the simpler one it grew out of (e.g. Talisman ADVANCED ← Talisman BASIC). The UI uses this to present related rulebooks as a set rather than a flat list, and to drive 'next step in the progression' navigation.

LegacyRunnerCapabilities.Description: Succession ledger for the legacy-runner promotion and its 2026-09-07 reversal. legacy-runner/ was a transitional staging area (2026-08-30 to 2026-09-07) for the root platform infrastructure (orchestrator, transpiler bus, execution substrates, conformance harness); it no longer exists as a directory, and that infrastructure is root infrastructure again. Each row records the capability, the original promote/separate/replace/retire decision, and — where the decision was reversed — an honest new decision and rationale. The admin portal capability was retired outright (deleted, not restored); every other reversed row is restored to root.

schema.name: LegacyRunnerCapabilityId
schema.Description: PK.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Order 1. Display alias (calculated).

schema.name: Title
schema.Description: Capability name.

schema.name: RunnerPath
schema.Description: Where the capability lives inside legacy-runner/.

schema.name: Summary
schema.Description: What the capability does.

schema.name: Decision
schema.Description: promote | separate | replace | retire.

schema.name: Destination
schema.Description: Who owns the behavior after retirement, or why nothing needs to.

schema.name: Rationale
schema.Description: Why this decision.

schema.name: Status
schema.Description: decided | in-progress | done. done means the successor exists and is wired; the runner keeps its copy regardless.

schema.name: Dependents
schema.Description: Known consumers that must be repointed before removal.

schema.name: Project
schema.Description: FK to ProjectMetadata.

schema.name: IsDecided
schema.Description: Order 1. A decision and a destination are both recorded.

schema.name: DecidedFlag
schema.Description: Order 1. 1 when decided — rollup carrier.

schema.name: IsKept
schema.Description: Order 1. The platform still needs the behavior (promote or separate).

schema.name: IsResolved
schema.Description: Order 1. The decision has been carried out.

schema.name: ResolvedFlag
schema.Description: Order 1. 1 when resolved — rollup carrier.

schema.name: CapabilityState
schema.Description: Order 2. undecided / decided / resolved.

schema.name: CapabilityLabel
schema.Description: Order 1. Display label with decision.

data.Rationale: The generated editor edits any rulebook with zero bespoke code and the explorer covers discovery and guidance; the portal's overlay contradicts one-rulebook-per-project.
data.Dependents: None outside the runner. Root start.sh has no dependency on it (US-052-ac1).

data.Title: Cross-project build tooling
data.Summary: Loops over every domain running effortless build and writes a status report.
data.Destination: scripts/scan-project-slots.py with ProjectSlotWitnesses / ConsistencyFindings views and the generated progress report.
data.Rationale: Repository status is now derived from witnessed slots and finding rows rather than a build loop's log.

data.Name: CLI orchestration menu
data.Title: CLI orchestration menu
data.RunnerPath: start.sh, orchestration/orchestrate.sh, run-web-portal.sh, run-in-docker.sh, docker-compose.yml, Dockerfile
data.Summary: Interactive menu that picks an active domain, builds it, runs substrates and launches the portal.
data.Destination: Is the root's own ./start.sh default (no flag needed); ./start.sh --portal launches the React explorer as the secondary web view.
data.Rationale: 2026-09-07: reversed. The CLI menu is not a legacy artifact kept alongside a newer default — it IS the new root's default entry point again. The React explorer remains real and useful as the --portal view, but the menu leads.

data.Name: Conformance harness and reports
data.Title: Conformance harness and reports
data.Summary: Blank tests, answer keys, per-substrate grading, fuzzy LLM grading and the substrate-equivalence report.
data.Destination: Conformance results as first-class rows in the root rulebook, displayed by the root explorer the way slot witnesses are; the runner keeps the harness and its report as the legacy view.
data.Rationale: Orchestration is what the explorer does visually: pick a project, build it, see every substrate graded. The harness stays runnable in the runner and its results become data the explorer shows.
data.Dependents: take-test.sh in every substrate; SubstrateContractPhases / EvaluationSteps rows in the runner rulebook. ConformanceRuns/ConformanceResults rows imported by scripts/run-conformance.py; displayed at /conformance in the root explorer.

data.Title: Devops scripts

data.Rationale: The hosted runner no longer exists; the root's launch contract covers restart and rebuild.

data.Name: Diagnostics and TSP research artifacts
data.Title: Diagnostics and TSP research artifacts

data.Destination: Stay in the runner as research history; no platform role.
data.Rationale: Research evidence, not platform behavior; nothing consumes it at runtime.

data.Title: Platform docs transpiler

data.Destination: rulebook-to-rulespeak, rulebook-to-progress-report and the root explorer, all registered in the root effortless.json.
data.Rationale: Bespoke doc generation duplicated what published transpilers now emit from the same rulebook.

data.Name: Execution substrates (injectors)
data.Title: Execution substrates (injectors)
data.Summary: Python, Go, COBOL, binary, CSV, XLSX, UML, OWL, English, explain-DAG, Airtable and postgres-calculated-to-rulebook injectors plus take-test harnesses.
data.Destination: Stays exactly where it is, now as root infrastructure: launched by the root's own ./start.sh, no longer staged for extraction into a separate governed project.
data.Rationale: 2026-09-07: the 2026-08-30 demotion that staged this for separation into its own project is reversed. External review read the demotion (this and the compiler/CLI/honest-conformance-matrix material moving four directories deep) as a credibility signal against evidence that had not actually changed. Promoting the runner back to root removes the reason to extract this component: it is root infrastructure again, not a legacy artifact awaiting relocation.

data.Name: Local transpiler bus
data.Title: Local transpiler bus
data.Summary: 11 repo-local injectors hosted as `script` tools by the effortless CLI on :4242. Replaced the hand-rolled ssotme-proxy HTTP server, which is deleted.
data.Destination: Absorbed by the effortless CLI (refactor Step 12). Each injector is a tool folder under effortless-tools/<name>/ whose transpiler.py calls orchestration/local_tool_shim.py; `effortless serve -port 4242` from the repo root hosts them all.
data.Rationale: 2026-09-12: the bus existed only to work around the old CLI POSTing an empty body -- ssotme-proxy had to identify the calling project by finding the CLI process behind the inbound TCP connection (lsof) and reading its cwd, which hard-coded the repo's folder layout and ignored the build step's own -i. CLI v2026.09.11.1616 hands a local tool its input directly (EFFORTLESS_INPUT_DIR), so the workaround has no remaining purpose. 395 lines of proxy deleted; all 16 enabled steps and acme-llc's 13/13 substrate conformance verified green on the native host.

ConformanceRuns.Description: One row per invocation of the cross-substrate conformance harness (orchestration/test-orchestrator.py) against a governed project. Imported by scripts/run-conformance.py from that project's testing/_substrate_results.json.

schema.name: ConformanceRunId
schema.Description: PK: run-<domain-slug>-<yyyymmdd-hhmmss>.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Order 1. Display alias (calculated).

schema.name: Domain
schema.Description: FK to the governed project this run tested.

schema.name: RanOn
schema.Description: ISO-8601 timestamp when the harness run was imported.

schema.name: RawResultsJson
schema.Description: JSON-encoded verbatim copy of the run's testing/_substrate_results.json, for audit/replay. Same string-blob convention as __meta__.JsonValue.

schema.name: DomainName
schema.Description: Order 1. Display name of the tested project.

schema.name: ConformanceResults
schema.Description: Reverse relationship: one row per substrate graded in this run.

schema.name: TotalSubstrates
schema.Description: Order 1. Substrates graded in this run.

schema.name: PassingSubstrateCount
schema.Description: Order 2. Substrates that passed (IsPassingFlag = 1) in this run.

schema.name: FailingSubstrateCount
schema.Description: Order 3. TotalSubstrates minus PassingSubstrateCount.

schema.name: OverallScore
schema.Description: Order 1. Average per-substrate score (0-100) across this run.

schema.name: OverallStatus
schema.Description: Order 4. no-results / all-passing / has-failures, derived from the substrate counts above.

schema.name: CorpusDomainRuns
schema.Description: Reverse relationship: the corpus-run attempt that produced this conformance run, when it came from a fan-out rather than a single-project run.

ConformanceResults.Description: One row per substrate graded within a ConformanceRuns run. Mirrors the per-substrate entries of testing/_substrate_results.json (last_run + last_successful_run.test_results) written by orchestration/test-orchestrator.py.

schema.name: ConformanceResultId
schema.Description: PK: <ConformanceRunId>:<substrate-name>.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Order 1. Display alias (calculated).

schema.name: Run
schema.Description: FK to the conformance run this substrate result belongs to.

schema.name: SubstrateName
schema.Description: Substrate key from _substrate_results.json (postgres, python, golang, owl, ...).

schema.name: Status
schema.Description: last_run.status from the harness: success or failure.

schema.name: Score
schema.Description: last_run.score (0-100) from the harness.

schema.name: FieldsTested
schema.Description: last_successful_run.test_results.total_fields_tested.

schema.name: FieldsPassed
schema.Description: last_successful_run.test_results.fields_passed.

schema.name: FieldsFailed
schema.Description: last_successful_run.test_results.fields_failed.

schema.name: DurationSeconds
schema.Description: last_run.duration_seconds.

schema.name: IsPassing
schema.Description: Order 2. True when the harness reported success at a perfect score.

schema.name: IsPassingFlag
schema.Description: Order 3. Numeric mirror of IsPassing (1/0) for SUMIFS rollups.

schema.name: RunDomainName
schema.Description: Order 4. Display name of the project this result's run tested.

TestSuites.Description: Registered test suites. One DECLARED row per suite the corpus runner is expected to execute: the repo-root formula-parser pytest suite plus one cross-substrate conformance suite per governed project. IsRegistered is a declaration, never inferred from the filesystem; the AnswerKeyCount / HasEffortlessJson / HasPostgresBootstrap columns are witnessed by scripts/scan-test-suites.py so RegistrationState can say WHY a registered suite is not yet runnable.

schema.name: TestSuiteId
schema.Description: PK: suite-<slug> for a project's conformance suite, suite-root-<name> for a root suite.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Order 1. Display alias (calculated).

schema.name: Domain
schema.Description: FK to the governed project this suite tests. Blank for repo-root suites that test the platform itself.

schema.name: SuiteKind
schema.Description: DECLARED. conformance (cross-substrate harness over a project) | pytest (a python test module at the repo root).

schema.name: Runner
schema.Description: DECLARED. The command that runs this suite, relative to the repo root.

schema.name: IsRegistered
schema.Description: DECLARED. This suite is part of the corpus the runner is expected to execute. An unregistered suite is skipped BY DECLARATION, never by accident.

schema.name: ExpectedSubstrateCount
schema.Description: DECLARED. How many execution substrates this suite should grade. 0 for pytest suites.

schema.name: Notes
schema.Description: Why this suite is (or is not yet) registered.

schema.name: AnswerKeyCount
schema.Description: WITNESSED by scan-test-suites.py: files in <project>/testing/answer-keys/.

schema.name: HasEffortlessJson
schema.Description: WITNESSED: the project has an effortless.json and can therefore be built.

schema.name: HasPostgresBootstrap
schema.Description: WITNESSED: postgres-bootstrap/reset-rulebook-db.sh exists, so the per-domain DB can be reset before grading.

schema.name: LastScannedOn
schema.Description: WITNESSED: ISO timestamp of the last scan-test-suites.py run that refreshed the witness fields.

schema.name: DomainName
schema.Description: Order 1. Display name of the tested project.

schema.name: DomainKind
schema.Description: Order 1. Declared kind (root | toy | example) of the tested project.

schema.name: HasAnswerKeys
schema.Description: Order 1. The project has at least one generated answer key.

schema.name: IsRunnable
schema.Description: Order 1. Registered AND buildable. This is the real gate on whether the runner attempts a suite; postgres-bootstrap/ and testing/answer-keys/ are GENERATED by the run itself, so their absence never blocks one.

schema.name: RunnableFlag
schema.Description: Order 1. 1 when IsRunnable, for SUMIFS rollups.

schema.name: IsGradable
schema.Description: Order 1. Runnable AND already carries answer keys, so this run can produce a conformance SCORE rather than generating its first key set.

schema.name: GradableFlag
schema.Description: Order 1. 1 when IsGradable, for SUMIFS rollups.

schema.name: RegistrationState
schema.Description: Order 1. Why this suite will or will not run: unregistered | no-effortless-json | never-exercised (runnable, but the first run generates its keys) | no-test-files | ready.

schema.name: CorpusDomainRuns
schema.Description: Reverse relationship: every corpus-run row that executed this suite.

schema.name: CorpusDomainRunCount
schema.Description: Order 1. How many corpus runs have executed this suite.

schema.name: HasBeenExercised
schema.Description: Order 1. Evidence on disk that this suite has been run at least once: generated answer keys or a generated postgres bootstrap. FALSE means the next run is this suite's first, not that it is broken.

schema.name: TestFileCount
schema.Description: WITNESSED: test_*.py files in a pytest suite's directory. Zero means the suite is registered but has nothing to run — which is how a platform test suite silently disappearing becomes visible in the registry instead of only as a red run.

CorpusRuns.Description: One row per corpus-wide fan-out (scripts/run-corpus.py). Append-only history: how much of the corpus was green on a given day is read straight off these rows.

schema.name: CorpusRunId
schema.Description: PK: corpus-<yyyymmdd>-<hhmmss>, matching the run directory under orchestration/corpus-runs/.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Order 1. Display alias (calculated).

schema.name: Mode
schema.Description: build-only (build + db reset, conformance skipped) | full (build + db reset + conformance).

schema.name: StartedOn
schema.Description: ISO timestamp the fan-out began.

schema.name: FinishedOn
schema.Description: ISO timestamp the fan-out finished. Blank while the run is still in flight.

schema.name: IsLatest
schema.Description: TRUE on exactly one row: the most recently STARTED corpus run. The runner clears it from every other row.

schema.name: TargetCount
schema.Description: How many suites the runner selected for this fan-out.

schema.name: StatusPath
schema.Description: Repo-relative path to this run's status.json, the live artifact the explorer tails.

schema.name: Notes
schema.Description: Free-text note about why this fan-out was run (baseline, post-fix re-run, ...).

schema.name: DomainRuns
schema.Description: Reverse relationship: one row per project attempted in this fan-out.

schema.name: DomainRunCount
schema.Description: Order 1. Projects attempted in this fan-out.

schema.name: GreenDomainCount
schema.Description: Order 2. Projects where no phase failed (a skipped phase does not fail a run).

schema.name: FullyGreenDomainCount
schema.Description: Order 2. Projects that BUILT and were CONFORMANCE-GRADED green — the number that matters for a full run.

schema.name: BuildFailureCount
schema.Description: Order 2. Projects whose build phase failed.

schema.name: DbFailureCount
schema.Description: Order 2. Projects whose database-reset phase failed.

schema.name: ConformanceFailureCount
schema.Description: Order 2. Projects whose conformance phase failed.

schema.name: TotalDurationSeconds
schema.Description: Order 1. Summed wall-clock of every project attempted.

schema.name: RedDomainCount
schema.Description: Order 3. Projects where at least one phase failed.

schema.name: GreenPercent
schema.Description: Order 3. Percentage of attempted projects with no failing phase.

schema.name: FullyGreenPercent
schema.Description: Order 3. Percentage of attempted projects that built AND graded green.

schema.name: IsComplete
schema.Description: Order 1. The fan-out has finished.

schema.name: IsCorpusGreen
schema.Description: Order 4. Every attempted project came back green.

schema.name: OverallStatus
schema.Description: Order 4. running | no-targets | green | red.

CorpusDomainRuns.Description: One row per (corpus run x project). Carries the per-phase outcome — build, database reset, conformance — so a red project is red for a NAMED phase instead of a grepped log line, and links to the ConformanceRuns row it produced.

schema.name: CorpusDomainRunId
schema.Description: PK: <CorpusRunId>:<project-slug>.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Order 1. Display alias (calculated).

schema.name: CorpusRun
schema.Description: FK to the fan-out this attempt belongs to.

schema.name: Domain
schema.Description: FK to the governed project attempted.

schema.name: Suite
schema.Description: FK to the registered test suite that was executed.

schema.name: BuildStatus
schema.Description: pass | fail | skipped — outcome of `effortless build` in the project directory.

schema.name: DbStatus
schema.Description: pass | fail | skipped — outcome of createdb + postgres-bootstrap/reset-rulebook-db.sh.

schema.name: ConformanceStatus
schema.Description: pass | fail | skipped — outcome of the cross-substrate harness.

schema.name: SubstratesTested
schema.Description: Substrates the harness graded in this attempt.

schema.name: SubstratesPassed
schema.Description: Substrates that scored 100 in this attempt.

schema.name: DurationSeconds
schema.Description: Wall-clock seconds for this project's whole attempt.

schema.name: FirstError
schema.Description: First error line captured from the failing phase. Blank when nothing failed.

schema.name: LogPath
schema.Description: Repo-relative path to this attempt's full log.

schema.name: ConformanceRun
schema.Description: FK to the ConformanceRuns row this attempt recorded, when the conformance phase ran.

schema.name: DomainName
schema.Description: Order 1. Display name of the attempted project.

schema.name: DomainKind
schema.Description: Order 1. Declared kind (root | toy | example) of the attempted project.

schema.name: CorpusRunMode
schema.Description: Order 1. Mode of the parent fan-out (build-only | full).

schema.name: CorpusRunIsLatest
schema.Description: Order 1. Flattened one hop so per-project 'green right now' can be a SUMIFS on this row.

schema.name: IsGreen
schema.Description: Order 1. No phase failed. A skipped phase does not fail an attempt.

schema.name: GreenFlag
schema.Description: Order 1. 1 when IsGreen, for SUMIFS rollups.

schema.name: IsFullyGreen
schema.Description: Order 1. Nothing failed AND conformance actually ran green — not merely 'nothing failed because nothing ran'. A pytest suite has no build phase, so this asks that the build did not FAIL rather than that it passed; a build-only attempt is never fully green because nothing was graded.

schema.name: FullyGreenFlag
schema.Description: Order 1. 1 when IsFullyGreen, for SUMIFS rollups.

schema.name: BuildFailedFlag
schema.Description: Order 1. 1 when the build phase failed.

schema.name: DbFailedFlag
schema.Description: Order 1. 1 when the database-reset phase failed.

schema.name: ConformanceFailedFlag
schema.Description: Order 1. 1 when the conformance phase failed.

schema.name: FailingPhase
schema.Description: Order 1. The first phase that failed, or blank when the attempt was green.

schema.name: LatestGreenFlag
schema.Description: Order 2. 1 when this attempt is green AND belongs to the latest fan-out. Flattens the two-hop 'is this project green right now' into one column.

schema.name: LatestFullyGreenFlag
schema.Description: Order 2. 1 when this attempt graded green with nothing failing AND belongs to the latest fan-out.

schema.name: LatestAttemptFlag
schema.Description: Order 2. 1 when this attempt belongs to the latest fan-out, green or not.

schema.name: ConformanceOutcome
schema.Description: Why the conformance phase landed where it did: all-substrates-passed | substrate-mismatch (the harness ran fine, substrates disagreed with the answer keys) | harness-error (the harness itself failed) | tests-passed / tests-failed (pytest suites) | skipped. RulebookFlavors.Description: Classification of each demo rulebook under rulebook-examples/. Lets the UI group projects by what they're TEACHING — a tutorial ladder is a different beast from a computation-heavy ontology. Density numbers come from a static analysis of each rulebook (calculated/aggregation/lookup counts).

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Order 1. Display alias (calculated). Order 1.

schema.name: SortOrder
schema.Description: Ascending integer; drives default display order in the portal. Lower = shown first. Tutorial-ladder projects sort before demos; demos before meta/graph.

schema.name: ProjectSlug
schema.Description: Folder under rulebook-examples/ — also the active-domain.txt value

schema.name: Domain
schema.Description: FK to RulebookDomains — the project directory this flavor card describes.

schema.name: Tagline
schema.description: One-sentence (~120 chars) summary used in the admin UI and as the rulebook Description.

schema.name: LogoPath
schema.description: Repo-relative path to the demo's effortless-logo.png (300x300, cartoon style).

schema.name: Flavor
schema.Description: crud-template | computation-heavy | aggregation-heavy | graph-ontology | meta-rulebook | tutorial-ladder

schema.name: Complexity
schema.Description: minimal | basic | advanced

schema.name: CalculatedCount
schema.Description: Number of calculated fields

schema.name: LearningFocus
schema.Description: What this demo is designed to teach

schema.name: GoodAnswerKeyFor
schema.Description: Substrate(s) this demo makes a particularly good answer-key witness for — when applicable

schema.name: FlavorTags
schema.Description: Reverse relationship: FlavorTags rows whose Flavor points here.

schema.name: DerivedFieldCount
schema.Description: Order 1. Calculated + aggregation + lookup fields.

schema.name: HasDomain
schema.Description: Order 1. Card is linked to an existing project directory.

schema.name: TagCount
schema.Description: Order 1. Tags attached to this card.

schema.name: AnswerKeyTargetCount
schema.Description: Order 1. Substrates listed as good answer keys.

schema.name: DomainArea
schema.Description: Order 1. Area of the linked domain.

schema.name: DerivedRatio
schema.Description: Order 2. Derived fields per entity.

schema.name: IsTagged
schema.Description: Order 2. Card carries at least one tag.

schema.name: IsToyFlavor
schema.Description: Order 2. Linked domain is a toy.

schema.name: DomainFindingCount
schema.Description: Order 2. Findings recorded against the linked domain.

schema.name: DomainOpenFindingCount
schema.Description: Order 3. Open findings on the linked domain.

schema.name: IsDenseDerivation
schema.Description: Order 3. At least one derived field per entity.

schema.name: IsCatalogComplete
schema.Description: Order 3. Linked to a real domain and tagged.

schema.name: DomainIsConsistent
schema.Description: Order 4. Whether the linked domain has no open findings.

schema.name: DomainIsStandardLayout
schema.Description: Order 4. Whether the linked domain's rulebook is at the canonical path.

schema.name: IsShowcaseCard
schema.Description: Order 4. Complete card whose domain has no open findings.

schema.name: IsCatalogReady
schema.Description: Order 5. Card and domain are both clean — safe to feature.

schema.name: DomainConformanceScore
schema.Description: Order 5. Conformance score of the linked domain.

FieldTypeTaxonomy.Description: Names every field-type the rulebook supports, with intent and example formula shape. Lets the UI explain what makes a calculated field different from a lookup field from an aggregation, instead of just showing a type tag.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Order 1. Display alias (calculated). Order 1.

schema.name: TypeName
schema.Description: The string that appears in schema[].type

schema.name: Intent
schema.Description: What this type is FOR — one sentence

schema.name: ExampleFormula
schema.Description: A representative formula or definition shape

schema.name: StorageMode
schema.Description: stored | derived-at-read | derived-at-write — where this field's value lives

schema.name: ReadOnlyInUi
schema.Description: True if the portal should never let users edit this field's value directly

schema.name: ExpressiveTier
schema.Description: Which substrate ExpressiveCompleteness tier is required to faithfully evaluate this — full | partial-formula | partial-aggregation | shape-only

schema.name: IsStored
schema.Description: Order 1. Field type is stored in the base table.

schema.name: IsFullyExpressiveTier
schema.Description: Order 1. Field type belongs to the full expressive tier.

schema.name: IsStoredAndEditable
schema.Description: Order 2. Stored and user-editable in the UI.

schema.name: TierLabel
schema.Description: Order 3. input / derived-full / derived-partial.

schema.name: IsInputTier
schema.Description: Order 4. User-entered field type.

schema.name: UiHint
schema.Description: Order 5. editable / read-only.

FormulaDialects.Description: Catalog of formula dialects that a rulebook can declare. Per-rulebook formula dialect is headline feature #6: each demo rulebook names which dialect it speaks (in _meta.formulaDialect), and substrates honor that declaration. The platform rulebook does not enumerate which functions a dialect supports — that lives in each demo rulebook's own formula definitions. This catalog only registers the dialects themselves.

schema.name: PrimarySubstrates

schema.name: Status
schema.Description: active | experimental | deprecated

schema.name: PrimarySubstrateCount
schema.Description: Order 1. Substrates listed as primary for this dialect.

schema.name: IsActiveMultiSubstrate

schema.name: DialectRole
schema.Description: Order 3. primary / niche / retired.

schema.name: IsPrimaryDialect
schema.Description: Order 4. Active dialect spanning several substrates.

schema.name: DialectLabel
schema.Description: Order 5. Display label marking the primary dialect.

data.Name: Airtable
data.Notes: Near-superset of Excel for the functions this project uses. Airtable-specific extensions (e.g. DATETIME_FORMAT) are honored when present.

data.Name: Excel
data.Notes: Default dialect for rulebooks without an explicit declaration. Covered by IF, AND, OR, CONCAT, LOWER, UPPER, SUBSTITUTE, LEFT, RIGHT, arithmetic, comparison.

DemoNarratives.Description: Curated narratives that demonstrate ERB capabilities in motion: substrates 'follow along' as the rulebook changes. Two narrative styles coexist: (1) commit-sequence narratives (legacy) where a single demo rulebook evolves over commits; (2) cross-rulebook narratives (current) where the same demo is observed across DIFFERENT rulebooks side-by-side. Cross-rulebook supersedes commit-sequence because RulebookDomains now form a tree (ParentDomainId) — the progression is data, not git history.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Order 1. Display alias (calculated). Order 1.

schema.name: Order

schema.name: NarrativeName

schema.name: RelatedDomainId

schema.name: ObservedCost

schema.name: NarrativeStyle

schema.name: Status
schema.Description: active | deprecated. Deprecated narratives are preserved for historical context but should not be used for new demos.

schema.name: SupersededBy
schema.Description: Name of the narrative that supersedes this one. Lossy soft reference: NarrativeName is shared by all step rows of a narrative, so this cannot be a single-row FK without a Narratives header table (future junction candidate).

schema.name: IsDeprecated
schema.Description: Order 1. Narrative step is deprecated.

schema.name: IsSuperseded
schema.Description: Order 1. A successor narrative is named.

schema.name: DomainName
schema.Description: Order 1. Name of the related domain.

schema.name: IsRetired
schema.Description: Order 2. Deprecated or superseded.

schema.name: DomainIsToy
schema.Description: Order 2. Whether the related domain is a toy.

schema.name: IsRetiredToyStory
schema.Description: Order 3. Retired narrative about a toy.

schema.name: IsLiveStory
schema.Description: Order 3. Current narrative bound to an existing domain.

schema.name: StoryState
schema.Description: Order 4. live / retired-toy / retired.

schema.name: IsCurrentStory
schema.Description: Order 5. Narrative still tells a current story.

data.Name: Substrate Drift (cross-rulebook progression) / CustomerFullName (root)
data.WhatHappens: Start at the simplest rulebook in the tree — one table, one CONCAT formula. Every substrate emits its analog. Conformance is 100% across the board.
data.KeyLesson: The contract is observable at minimum scale. A 1-table rulebook is enough to exercise inject + execute + grade end-to-end.

data.Name: Substrate Drift (cross-rulebook progression) / Talisman BASIC (child of root)
data.WhatHappens: Walk down the progression tree to Talisman BASIC — adds relationships, aggregations, role/agent separation. Every substrate handles the elaboration with no substrate-side edits. [Referenced demo talisman-basic has been removed from the repo.]
data.KeyLesson: Walking the tree of rulebooks (ParentDomainId) IS the demo — no git rewind required. The viewer can see N rulebooks side-by-side rather than replaying commits.

data.Name: Substrate Drift (cross-rulebook progression) / Talisman ADVANCED (child of BASIC)
data.WhatHappens: Walk further down: Talisman ADVANCED elaborates BASIC with cross-entity lookups and conditional IF logic. Conformance still 100% across deterministic substrates. [Referenced demo talisman-advanced has been removed from the repo.]
data.KeyLesson: Elaboration within a tree of rulebooks costs the SAME as elaboration within a commit history — proving that 'commits' was never the load-bearing thing; the progression structure was.

data.Name: Substrate Drift (cross-rulebook progression) / Star Trek (sibling root)
data.WhatHappens: Jump to a sibling root in the tree — different domain entirely. Deterministic substrates regenerate and conform. The English substrate is 100% stale until regenerated.
data.KeyLesson: Cross-rulebook navigation makes the 'domain swap' observable as a tree traversal, not a git checkout. Same lesson as the legacy commit-sequence demo, but now data-driven.

data.Name: Substrate Drift (BASIC → ADVANCED → NEW ONTOLOGY) / BASIC
data.WhatHappens: All substrates pass at 100% on a 9-table workflow ontology with relationships, aggregations, and boolean derivations. [Referenced demo talisman-basic has been removed from the repo.]
data.KeyLesson: Substrates have wildly different regeneration costs even at full conformance.

data.Name: Substrate Drift (BASIC → ADVANCED → NEW ONTOLOGY) / ADVANCED
data.WhatHappens: Rename and modify elements within the same ontology — add cross-entity lookups and conditional logic. Every substrate follows along with no edits to substrate code. [Referenced demo talisman-advanced has been removed from the repo.]
data.KeyLesson: Interface changes propagate automatically. This is the polymorphism payoff.
data.ObservedCost: Cost profile unchanged from BASIC — work is in the rulebook, not in substrate code.

data.Name: Substrate Drift (BASIC → ADVANCED → NEW ONTOLOGY) / NEW ONTOLOGY
data.WhatHappens: Swap to an entirely different domain (e.g. star-trek media catalog). Deterministic substrates regenerate and conform. The English substrate is now 100% wrong against the new answer key until its prose is regenerated by the LLM.
data.KeyLesson: The static English content is 100% stale across domain swaps. Regenerating it costs time and money — the dominant cost lives in the slowest substrate, not in the rulebook.
data.ObservedCost: Deterministic substrates < 1s; English regeneration ~5min and ~$0.10-$1 in LLM tokens.

Glossary.Description: Authoritative glossary for the ERB platform. Every term used in orchestration code, docs, the admin portal UI, or rulebook tables appears here EXACTLY ONCE, with a definition AND an ImplementedAs pointer back into this rulebook (or to source files when the implementation is code rather than data). If a term appears in repo prose but has no row here, that's a documentation bug. If a term has a row here but no ImplementedAs target, that's an architecture bug — every concept should be data, code, or a value.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Order 1. Display alias (calculated). Order 1.

schema.name: Term
schema.Description: The canonical word/phrase as it appears in code and docs.

schema.name: Category
schema.Description: concept | role | artifact | phase | substrate | dimension | pattern | tool | location | invariant — what KIND of thing this term refers to.

schema.name: Definition
schema.Description: One precise sentence. Do not restate the term itself.

schema.name: ImplementedAs
schema.Description: Pointer to where this term is realized: 'table:X', 'column:X.Y', 'value:X.Y=Z', 'file:path/to/file', or 'axiom:axiom-id'. The promise is that a reader can follow this pointer and find the concept's actual realization.

schema.name: Aliases
schema.Description: Comma-separated other names that should resolve to this term. The canonical spelling is in Term; aliases redirect to it.

schema.name: AliasCount
schema.Description: Order 1. Number of aliases listed.

schema.name: HasImplementation
schema.Description: Order 1. Term points at a concrete implementation.

schema.name: ImplementationKind
schema.Description: Order 1. Prefix of ImplementedAs before the colon (file, table, script ...); blank when none.

schema.name: IsFileBacked
schema.Description: Order 2. Implemented as a file path.

schema.name: IsRichTerm
schema.Description: Order 2. Has aliases and an implementation pointer.

schema.name: TermQuality
schema.Description: Order 3. anchored / rich / implemented / definition-only.

schema.name: IsAnchored
schema.Description: Order 4. Rich term anchored to a file.

schema.name: GlossaryTier
schema.Description: Order 5. tier-1 / tier-2 / tier-3.

data.Name: Active Domain
data.Definition: The currently-selected demo rulebook project. Recorded in orchestration/active-domain.txt; consulted by every orchestration script.

data.Name: Add Tool
data.Definition: Catalog of transpilers the developer can install into the active project from the admin portal.

data.Name: Admin Portal
data.Definition: Local web app on :7777 that edits the active project's rulebook. Categorically NOT a domain — like Word vs. a .docx (see CLAUDE.md).

data.Name: Aggregation Field
data.Definition: A calculated field that summarizes many related rows (SUM, COUNT, ARRAY).

data.Name: airtable-to-rulebook
data.Definition: Transpiler that pulls Airtable schema and data INTO the rulebook JSON. An input spoke. Disabled by default; explicit consent required.
data.Notes: See CLAUDE.md — Airtable pull is disabled by default.

data.Name: answer-key.json
data.Definition: The canonical expected values, derived directly from rulebook seed data — never from a substrate. The oracle for grading.
data.Notes: If answer-key comes from a substrate, that's a privileged-substrate bug (ax-002).

data.Name: AppAPI
data.Definition: An HTTP route on the admin portal backend, governed by AppPermissions.

data.Name: AppNavigation
data.Definition: Tree of navigation entries driving the admin portal sidebar.

data.Name: AppPermission
data.Definition: Declarative per-(role, route) allow/deny rule for the admin portal API surface.

data.Name: AppScreen
data.Definition: A named screen in the admin portal, with declared entity reads/writes.

data.Name: AppUser
data.Definition: A user account for the admin portal, declared in the rulebook (not in a separate auth DB).

data.Name: Axiom
data.Definition: A positive-form invariant the project is built on; load-bearing — if dropped, the methodology no longer holds.

data.Name: blank-test.json
data.Definition: The exam: rows with raw fields populated and all computed fields nulled. Every substrate in a run receives the same blank-test.

data.Name: Build Pipeline
data.Definition: The effortless.json contract describing input rulebook + list of project transpilers, consumed by both the portal and the CLI.

data.Name: Calculated Field
data.Definition: A field whose value is computed from a formula over other fields in the same row. Filled in by each substrate's generated Calc*() function.

data.Name: CanBeAnswerKey
data.Definition: Property of a substrate: whether its output is structurally complete enough to serve as the oracle in a conformance run. NOT a trust ranking.

data.Name: Click Target
data.Definition: A canonical clickable affordance in the portal — every interactive element MUST resolve to a row here.

data.Name: CMCC
data.Definition: Conjecture: a sufficiently expressive rulebook can be projected into ANY substrate while preserving identical observable behavior. The conjecture ERB tests.

data.Name: Conformance
data.Definition: The property that all substrates compute IDENTICAL field-level values from the same rulebook + blank-test. Measured per-run.

data.Name: Demo Narrative
data.Definition: A scripted sequence of demo steps illustrating substrate behavior under rulebook change. Two styles: commit-sequence (legacy) and cross-rulebook (current).

data.Name: Demo Rulebook
data.Definition: A per-domain rulebook under rulebook-examples/ that captures one business ontology. Categorically not the platform rulebook.

data.Name: Determinism
data.Definition: Reproducibility class of a substrate: deterministic | stochastic | externally-influenced.

data.Name: Domain-agnostic
data.Definition: Property of orchestration code: contains ZERO words from any business domain (no 'customer', 'workflow', 'episode'). Translates generic rulebook structures only.
data.Notes: Violation = domain leak.

data.Name: effortless CLI
data.Definition: Command-line front end (`effortless build`, `-init`, `-install`) that drives the build pipeline. Also known as ssotme/aicapture/aic.

data.Name: effortless.json
data.Definition: Per-project configuration file naming the rulebook input and the list of project transpilers (with their proxy URLs).

data.Name: effortless-platform/
data.Definition: Folder containing the platform itself as an Effortless project — the orchestration tool 'eating its own dog food'.

data.Name: Evaluation Artifact
data.Definition: A file flowing between phases of the contract (rulebook, blank-test, test-answers, answer-key, test-results, substrate artifact).

data.Name: Evaluation Step
data.Definition: A substep within a SubstrateContractPhase (e.g. load rulebook, walk entities, compile formulas).

data.Name: Execute
data.Definition: Phase 2 of the substrate contract: run blank-test.json through the substrate's generated functions and emit test-answers.json.

data.Name: execution-substrates/
data.Definition: Folder containing each local substrate's injector + take-test scripts.

data.Name: Expressive Completeness
data.Definition: Which formula classes a substrate can faithfully evaluate: full | partial-aggregation | partial-formula | shape-only.

data.Name: Field Type
data.Definition: The kind of field on a rulebook table: raw, calculated, lookup, aggregation, relationship.

data.Name: Formula Dialect
data.Definition: The flavor of formula language a rulebook declares (Excel, Airtable, …). Substrates honor the declaration; substrate-specific extensions are an error.

data.Name: Framing Invariant
data.Definition: A wrong framing of the project that has been caught and is now blocked. Mistake-to-avoid catalog; the contrapositive of an axiom.

data.Name: Fuzzy Grader
data.Definition: LLM-based grader for the English substrate — the only non-deterministic substrate. Uses one of the FuzzyGradingProviders.

data.Name: Grade
data.Definition: Phase 3 of the substrate contract: compare every substrate's test-answers.json against the canonical answer-key.json, field by field.

data.Name: Hub
data.Definition: The rulebook JSON acting as the SSoT center; all inputs (Airtable, LLM edits, admin portal saves) write INTO it and all outputs (substrates) read FROM it.

data.Name: Inject
data.Definition: Phase 1 of the substrate contract: read the rulebook and emit a runnable substrate artifact (SDK / schema / workbook).

data.Name: Injector
data.Definition: A per-substrate Python script that reads the rulebook JSON and emits the substrate artifact. Must contain ZERO domain words to remain domain-agnostic.
data.Notes: See SubstrateContractPhases.phase-inject.FailureMode.

data.Name: Input Spoke
data.Definition: A peer that writes into the rulebook JSON: admin portal save, Airtable pull, LLM-direct edit, hand-edit.

data.Name: licensed-effortless-tools/
data.Definition: Folder where the licensed Effortless transpilers (Postgres, Excel, Entity Framework) land their outputs.

data.Name: Lookup Field
data.Definition: A calculated field that resolves a value from a related row in another table.

data.Name: Maturity
data.Definition: Per-substrate implementation completeness: prototype | demonstrating | reference-quality. Independent of TranspilerSource.

data.Name: No Fallback Rule
data.Definition: Repo-wide policy: if a file is missing, fail loudly with the exact expected path. No silent path-guessing, no try/except that swallows missing files. Defaults derived deterministically from the SSoT are not fallbacks.

data.Name: orchestration/
data.Definition: Folder holding the build/test runners that drive every demo: orchestrate.sh, shared.py, formula_parser.py, test-orchestrator.py, generate-report.py, active-domain.txt.

data.Name: Output Spoke
data.Definition: A substrate that reads from the rulebook JSON to produce a derived artifact. Plural; the rulebook drives N output spokes per project.

data.Name: Parent Domain
data.Definition: The simpler rulebook a more-elaborate one was derived from. Forms the progression tree of demos.

data.Name: Platform Rulebook
data.Definition: The single rulebook that describes the ERB orchestration tool ITSELF — admin portal, build pipeline, substrates, framing invariants. Distinct from demo rulebooks; the parent, not a sibling.
data.Notes: See CLAUDE.md — THE PROJECT RULEBOOK ≠ A DEMO RULEBOOK.

data.Name: Portal/CLI Parity
data.Definition: Admin portal and `./start.sh --cli` are peers over the same effortless.json pipeline. Anything one can do, the other can do; behavior cannot diverge.

data.Name: Privileged Substrate
data.Definition: An anti-pattern: treating one substrate (e.g. Airtable, Postgres) as the authoritative oracle rather than a peer. Forbidden by ax-002.

data.Name: Raw Field
data.Definition: A field whose value is stored, not computed. Populated by input spokes; carried through unchanged by every substrate.

data.Name: Role-Screen Hint
data.Definition: Per-(role, screen) UX override on top of the base AppScreens definition.

data.Name: Rulebook
data.Definition: A single JSON file (effortless-rulebook.json or <domain>-rulebook.json) that declaratively encodes the schema, formulas, and seed data for one project; the durable SSoT from which every substrate is mechanically derived.

data.Name: Rulebook Domain
data.Definition: One demo ontology under rulebook-examples/. Domains form a tree via ParentDomainId.

data.Name: rulebook-examples/
data.Definition: Folder containing N independent demo Effortless projects, each its own rulebook + effortless.json + outputs.

data.Name: Rulebook Flavor
data.Definition: Classification of a demo rulebook (business, philosophical, self-referential, etc.) so the UI can group related demos.

data.Name: Rulebook Promotion
data.Definition: The architectural decision to promote effortless-rulebook.json from disposable IR to durable hub/SSoT, demoting Airtable from authority to peer input spoke. Largely complete.

data.Name: rulebook-to-airtable
data.Definition: Reverse-sync transpiler that pushes rulebook changes BACK to Airtable. An output spoke (Airtable becomes a downstream view).

data.Name: rulebook-to-postgres
data.Definition: Licensed Effortless transpiler that generates DDL, stored functions, and views from the rulebook. Reference-quality substrate output.

data.Name: Runtime Kind
data.Definition: What kind of artifact a substrate produces / runs as: database | spreadsheet | binary | text-emit | graph | docs.

data.Name: Spoke
data.Definition: Any peer system connected to the hub — either an input spoke writing into the rulebook, or an output spoke (substrate) reading from it.

data.Name: SSoT
data.Definition: Single Source of Truth. The rulebook JSON is the durable SSoT; every other artifact is mechanically rederivable.
data.Aliases: single source of truth, source of truth

data.Name: Local transpiler host
data.Definition: The effortless CLI's own host for this repo's tools, on 127.0.0.1:4242. It serves every folder under effortless-tools/ as a transpiler route and hands each tool its input directly. Replaced the hand-rolled ssotme-proxy server on 2026-09-12.
data.Aliases: local tool host, transpiler bus, effortless serve

data.Name: Local Tool Route
data.Definition: A route on the local transpiler host (e.g. POST /oss-rulebook-to-python) that invokes the matching injector with ERB_RULEBOOK_PATH and ERB_OUTPUT_DIR.

data.Name: Substrate
data.Definition: An execution environment — language, database, spreadsheet, ontology, binary — into which the rulebook is mechanically projected. All substrates are peers (ax-002).

data.Name: take-test
data.Definition: A per-substrate script that runs blank-test.json through the substrate's generated functions and emits test-answers.json.

data.Name: test-answers.json
data.Definition: A substrate's exam answers — blank-test with that substrate's computed values filled in.

data.Name: Test Orchestrator
data.Definition: The orchestration-level script that loads answer-key.json, collects each substrate's test-answers.json, compares them, and emits the grade report.

data.Name: test-results
data.Definition: Field-level diff report (Markdown) comparing each substrate's test-answers.json to answer-key.json.

data.Name: Substrate Tradeoff
data.Definition: A per-(substrate × dimension) Pro/Con/Note record. The matrix is complete: every substrate is rated on every dimension.

data.Name: Tradeoff Dimension
data.Definition: One axis of comparison applied to every substrate (speed, accuracy, debuggability, …).

data.Name: Transpiler Source
data.Definition: Provenance of a substrate's generator: licensed-effortless-tool | local-injector | external. WHO built it, not how trustworthy it is.
data.Notes: See FramingInvariants.framing-003.

data.Name: User Role
data.Definition: An admin-portal access tier (Viewer, Developer, …). Each role is a PERSONA with a landing screen and a permission set.

data.Name: Write-Through Invariant
data.Definition: Every admin-portal save writes to BOTH Postgres (live editor) AND the rulebook JSON (durable SSoT) in the same logical transaction.

ClaudeSkills.Description: The catalog of Claude Code skills that make up the effortless-skills skill set (repo renamed from effortless-claude). Each skill is a loadable instruction set that pre-teaches Claude everything it needs to work in an ERB project — naming conventions, pipeline mechanics, formula semantics, etc. Skills are the answer to the LLM learning-curve problem: instead of every user teaching Claude from scratch, the learning is encoded once and loaded on demand. LocalMirrorPath is a derived artifact: clone-skills.sh pulls a live copy of each skill from the source repo so the docs/skills/ mirror stays current.
