UserStories.Description: User stories of the repo-consistency programme (progress-report contract).

schema.name: UserStoryId
schema.Description: PK.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Order 1. Display alias (calculated). Order 1.

schema.name: ReqId
schema.Description: Requirement code shown in the report (US-001 ...).

schema.name: StoryText
schema.Description: As a <persona>, I want <capability>, so <outcome>.

schema.name: BuildPhase
schema.Description: FK to BuildPhases.

schema.name: Epic
schema.Description: FK to ERBFeatureCategories. Read directly by the report (not inferred via Feature).

schema.name: Feature
schema.Description: FK to ERBFeatures.

schema.name: EffortClass
schema.Description: FK to EffortClasses (G1/G2/G3).

schema.name: Status
schema.Description: todo | in-progress | done (asserted by the team).

schema.name: DevProgressPercent
schema.Description: Asserted developer progress 0-100 (read by the progress-report tool).

schema.name: AcceptanceCriteria
schema.Description: Reverse relationship: criteria of this story.

schema.name: CriterionCount
schema.Description: Order 1. Acceptance criteria attached.

schema.name: IsDone
schema.Description: Order 1. Team asserts the story is done.

schema.name: DoneFlag
schema.Description: Order 1. 1 when done — rollup carrier.

schema.name: EffortWeight
schema.Description: Order 1. Complexity weight of the effort class.

schema.name: PhaseNumber
schema.Description: Order 1. Number of the scheduled phase.

schema.name: FeatureTitle
schema.Description: Order 1. Title of the feature.

schema.name: MetCriterionCount
schema.Description: Order 2. Acceptance criteria currently met.

schema.name: HasCriteria
schema.Description: Order 2. Story carries acceptance criteria.

schema.name: WeightedDone
schema.Description: Order 2. Effort weight earned if done, else 0.

schema.name: DerivedProgressPercent
schema.Description: Order 3. Progress derived from met criteria; falls back to the asserted percent only when a story has no criteria.

schema.name: IsAcceptanceComplete
schema.Description: Order 3. Every criterion is met.

schema.name: HasStatusDrift
schema.Description: Order 3. Asserted done while criteria remain unmet.

schema.name: WeightedProgress
schema.Description: Order 4. Derived progress times effort weight.

schema.name: ProgressState
schema.Description: Order 4. drift / accepted / in-flight / not-started.

schema.name: PriorityBand
schema.Description: Order 5. fix-first / continue / queue.

schema.name: ReportLabel
schema.Description: Order 5. Display label with progress state.

data.Name: US-001
data.StoryText: As a platform maintainer, I want every project directory under rulebook-examples/ and toy-rulebooks/ modeled as a RulebookDomains row keyed by its slug, so the catalog and the filesystem can never silently diverge.

data.Name: US-002
data.StoryText: As a demo author, I want each domain row to carry its actual rulebook path and table count, so stale documentation references are queryable facts instead of folklore.

data.Name: US-003
data.StoryText: As a platform maintainer, I want substrates, proxy routes, transpiler tools, skills, glossary terms, axioms and framing invariants each in a first-class table, so every semantic concept in the repo has exactly one home.

data.Name: US-004
data.StoryText: As an agent working the repo, I want the skill catalog reconciled to the installed skill set including deprecations, so routing decisions come from data, not memory.

data.Name: US-005
data.StoryText: As a rulebook tender, I want every implicit foreign key (XxxId strings) materialized as a typed relationship with an inverse field, so lookups and aggregations have real edges to traverse.

data.Name: US-006
data.StoryText: As a rulebook tender, I want table-level cycles broken deliberately and documented, so the DAG stays acyclic on purpose rather than by accident.

data.Name: US-007
data.StoryText: As a platform maintainer, I want five breadth-first inference loops across every table, so the governing rulebook demonstrates the ~50/50 raw/derived ratio the platform preaches.

data.Name: US-008
data.StoryText: As a reviewer, I want every derived field labeled with its inference order and an honest description, so the loop discipline is auditable.

data.Name: US-009
data.StoryText: As a repo visitor, I want every demo rulebook at <slug>/effortless-rulebook/<slug>-rulebook.json, so one glob finds every ontology.

data.Name: US-010
data.StoryText: As a maintainer, I want duplicate rulebook copies removed, so there is exactly one hub per project.

data.Name: US-011
data.StoryText: As a maintainer, I want committed scratch artifacts purged and gitignored, so the repo only carries hubs, customization seams and intentional derivatives.

data.Name: US-012
data.StoryText: As a maintainer, I want the nested git repository in lazr-coulombs-law dissolved into the monorepo, so one git history governs every project.

data.Name: US-013
data.StoryText: As a demo reader, I want the rulespeak transpiler registered in every demo effortless.json, so every domain has a human-readable narrative output.

data.Name: US-014
data.StoryText: As a maintainer, I want duplicate and misspelled transpiler names fixed, so effortless.json entries are unique and greppable.

data.Name: US-015
data.StoryText: As a maintainer, I want every project to carry a real effortless.json, so effortless build works from any project root.

data.Name: US-016
data.StoryText: As a maintainer, I want legacy ssotme.json files retired, so there is one config file per project.

data.Name: US-017
data.StoryText: As a repo visitor, I want a README in every project, so no directory is a mystery.

data.Name: US-018
data.StoryText: As a repo visitor, I want every README to end with the local-transpiler-bus section, so the localhost:4242 route catalog is discoverable from any demo.

data.Name: US-019
data.StoryText: As a platform consumer, I want every rulebook to carry the typed-row __meta__ table, so metaAsObject() works uniformly.

data.Name: US-020
data.StoryText: As an agent reading CLAUDE.md, I want doctrine examples to match the filesystem, so instructions never point at directories that do not exist.

data.Name: US-021
data.StoryText: As a programme owner, I want the eight required progress-report tables present with the exact contract fields, so rulebook-to-progress-report renders without hand-editing.

data.Name: US-022
data.StoryText: As a programme owner, I want the contract guardrails honored in data, so the tool's hard refusals never fire.

data.Name: US-023
data.StoryText: As a stakeholder, I want the full consistency programme expressed as user stories with acceptance criteria, so progress is measured against agreed scope.

data.Name: US-024
data.StoryText: As a stakeholder, I want stories to carry status and progress percent, so the report reflects live reality.

data.Name: US-025
data.StoryText: As a stakeholder, I want story→feature→epic→package→phase rollups computed as derived fields, so progress math lives in the SSoT, not in a spreadsheet.

data.Name: US-026
data.StoryText: As a stakeholder, I want rulebook-to-progress-report registered in the platform pipeline, so the report regenerates on every build.

data.Name: US-027
data.StoryText: As a stakeholder, I want the generated progress report linked from the root explorer, so it is one tap away without using the legacy portal.

data.Name: US-028
data.StoryText: As a visitor, I want one responsive navigation shell for the root explorer, so the same platform guide works on phones and desktops.

data.Name: US-029
data.StoryText: As a visitor, I want the root explorer navigation plan stored as rulebook rows, so navigation changes originate in the hub.

data.Name: US-030
data.StoryText: As a visitor, I want every planned explorer screen mapped or consciously excluded from the route model, so no platform concept is stranded.

data.Name: US-031
data.StoryText: As a phone visitor, I want lists, tables, and navigation adapted responsively, so nothing requires horizontal page scrolling.

data.Name: US-032
data.StoryText: As an explorer, I want deep-linkable routes for getting started, concepts, skills, toys, examples, projects, and tools modeled as data, so any destination can be shared.

data.Name: US-033
data.StoryText: As an explorer, I want the custom root React app implemented against this rulebook's vw_ views, so classifications, counts, readiness, and priorities are never recomputed in JavaScript.

data.Name: US-034
data.StoryText: As a governance reader, I want routes for the governing rulebook, axioms, invariants, consistency, findings, and progress, so the repository explains how it governs itself.

data.Name: US-035
data.StoryText: As a maintainer, I want the root explorer's findings queue filterable by project, rule, and status at any viewport, so sweep triage is practical.

data.Name: US-036
data.StoryText: As a maintainer, I want a root-explorer work-queue screen reading vw_consistency_findings, so pruning inconsistency is ticking rows off, not re-auditing.

data.Name: US-037
data.StoryText: As a stakeholder, I want a root consistency dashboard showing per-project scores from derived fields, so repository health is visible at a glance.

data.Name: US-038
data.StoryText: As a catalog curator, I want every flavor card FK-linked to its domain row, so orphan cards and cardless domains are queryable.

data.Name: US-039
data.StoryText: As a catalog curator, I want a flavor card for every non-exception domain, so the catalog page represents the whole repo.

data.Name: US-040
data.StoryText: As a catalog curator, I want FlavorTags joined through real FKs, so tag orphans surface as derived flags.

data.Name: US-041
data.StoryText: As a catalog curator, I want every RulebookTag used at least once or retired, so the tag vocabulary stays honest.

data.Name: US-042
data.StoryText: As an agent, I want ClaudeSkills to mirror the installed skill set with load gates and status, so skill discovery is data-driven.

data.Name: US-043
data.StoryText: As a skills maintainer, I want the skills repo, the installed set and this table checked for drift at build time, so divergence is caught, not discovered.

data.Name: US-044
data.StoryText: As an agent, I want the orchestrator's routing table modeled as SkillRoutes edges, so "which skill next" is a query.

data.Name: US-045
data.StoryText: As a skills maintainer, I want every SKILL.md see-also cross-reference round-tripped into SkillRoutes, so the meta-conversation inside the skill set is part of this rulebook.

data.Name: US-046
data.StoryText: As a repository visitor, I want the root and every governed toy and example to have an executable ./start.sh, so every project has the same obvious launch command.

data.Name: US-047
data.StoryText: As a new visitor, I want the root ./start.sh to start the platform explorer and required view-backed services, so the repository has one supported entry point.

data.Name: US-048
data.StoryText: As an explorer, I want every project page to show exact launch instructions and a health-gated localhost link when available, so running a project requires no source-code archaeology.

data.Name: US-049
data.StoryText: As a first-time visitor, I want the root explorer to explain setup, concepts, skills, toys, and fully implemented examples, so I can understand the platform and choose what to run.

data.Name: US-050
data.StoryText: As a rulebook tender, I want the root explorer to link prominently to the generated editor, RuleSpeak, and API health, so the custom guide complements rather than replaces generated surfaces.

data.Name: US-051
data.StoryText: As a platform maintainer, I want every legacy-runner capability assigned a promote, separate, replace, or retire decision naming its successor, so the runner can stay an ordinary example without any platform role silently depending on it.

data.Name: US-052
data.StoryText: As a platform maintainer, I want the root experience independent of the legacy portal and two-rulebook overlay, so the promoted platform has one explicit owner while legacy-runner remains an ordinary governed example.

data.Name: US-053
data.StoryText: As a repository maintainer, I want the canonical project shape and strict filesystem witnesses modeled in the root rulebook, so coverage, readiness, classification, misfiling, and structural findings are derived rather than asserted.

data.Name: US-054
data.StoryText: As an explorer, I want launch instructions and localhost health contracts modeled as first-class rulebook rows, so the application never scrapes shell text or invents a URL.

AcceptanceCriteria.Description: Acceptance criteria per user story (progress-report contract).

schema.name: AcceptanceCriterionId
schema.Description: PK.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Order 1. Display alias (calculated). Order 1.

schema.name: UserStory
schema.Description: FK to UserStories.

schema.name: Criterion
schema.Description: Testable statement that must hold for the story to be accepted.

schema.name: IsMet
schema.Description: Witnessed: the criterion currently holds.

schema.name: MetFlag
schema.Description: Order 1. 1 when met — rollup carrier.

schema.name: StoryReqId
schema.Description: Order 1. ReqId of the owning story.

schema.name: StoryStatus
schema.Description: Order 1. Asserted status of the owning story.

schema.name: StoryIsDone
schema.Description: Order 2. Whether the owning story is asserted done.

schema.name: StoryCriterionCount
schema.Description: Order 2. Sibling criteria count.

schema.name: IsInconsistentWithStory
schema.Description: Order 3. Story says done but this criterion is not met.

schema.name: ShareOfStory
schema.Description: Order 3. Percent of the story this criterion represents.

schema.name: StoryDerivedProgress
schema.Description: Order 4. Criteria-derived progress of the owning story.

schema.name: CriterionState
schema.Description: Order 4. contradicts-story / met / pending.

schema.name: NeedsReview
schema.Description: Order 5. Contradicts the story's asserted status.

schema.name: StoryIsAheadOfCriterion
schema.Description: Order 5. Story is over half done while this criterion is still pending.

data.Name: canonical-rulebook-path
data.Statement: Every project's rulebook lives directly in <project>/effortless-rulebook/, named either effortless-rulebook.json or <slug>-rulebook.json (both valid; the protocol does not dictate one).
data.CheckMechanism: Compare RulebookDomains.RulebookPath against RelativePath + "effortless-rulebook/" + either accepted filename (RulebookDomains.IsStandardLayout).
data.FixPlaybook: git mv the file into effortless-rulebook/ under either accepted name; update effortless.json -i/-o arguments; rebuild.
data.SourceDoctrine: CLAUDE.md § Two categorically different kinds of rulebooks

data.Name: effortless-json-present
data.Statement: Every project directory carries a real effortless.json build configuration.
data.CheckMechanism: test -f <project>/effortless.json and confirm it has a ProjectTranspilers array.
data.FixPlaybook: effortless -init from the project root, then register transpilers with effortless -install.

data.Name: rulespeak-registered
data.Statement: Every demo effortless.json includes a rulebooktorulespeak ProjectTranspilers entry.
data.CheckMechanism: jq '.ProjectTranspilers[].Name' effortless.json | grep rulebooktorulespeak
data.FixPlaybook: cd rulespeak && effortless -install rulebook-to-rulespeak -i ../effortless-rulebook/<slug>-rulebook.json
data.SourceDoctrine: CLAUDE.md § Required transpilers for every new example project

data.Name: readme-present
data.Statement: Every project directory has a README.md.
data.CheckMechanism: test -f <project>/README.md
data.FixPlaybook: Write a README: purpose, layout, how to build, then the bus section.

data.Name: readme-bus-section
data.Statement: Every README ends with the "## Local transpiler bus (`127.0.0.1:4242`)" section with the current transpiler count.
data.CheckMechanism: tail README.md | grep "Local transpiler bus"
data.FixPlaybook: Append the canonical block from CLAUDE.md.

data.Name: meta-table-present
data.Statement: Every rulebook carries a typed-row __meta__ table and no project metadata outside it.
data.CheckMechanism: jq 'has("__meta__")' <rulebook>
data.FixPlaybook: python3 orchestration/migrate-meta-to-table.py <rulebook>

data.Name: single-hub-per-project
data.Statement: Exactly one rulebook JSON is the hub of a project; no duplicate copies at other paths.
data.CheckMechanism: find <project> -name "*rulebook*.json" -not -path "*/node_modules/*" | wc -l == 1 (derived files excepted)
data.FixPlaybook: Delete the copy that effortless.json does not reference.
data.SourceDoctrine: CLAUDE.md § Authoritative Source: rulebook JSON is HEAD

data.Name: no-committed-scratch
data.Statement: No scratch/build artifacts (.bak, __pycache__, node_modules, *.log, lockfiles without manifests) are tracked in git.
data.CheckMechanism: git ls-files <project> | grep -E "\.bak$|__pycache__|node_modules|\.log$"
data.FixPlaybook: git rm --cached and add to .gitignore.

data.Name: no-nested-git
data.Statement: No project directory is its own git repository.
data.CheckMechanism: find . -mindepth 2 -name .git -type d
data.FixPlaybook: Remove the nested .git (archive history if needed) so the monorepo tracks the files.

data.Name: unique-transpiler-names
data.Statement: Within one effortless.json, every ProjectTranspilers entry has a unique Name.
data.CheckMechanism: jq '.ProjectTranspilers[].Name' | sort | uniq -d
data.FixPlaybook: Rename the duplicate (e.g. rulebooktorulespeakde, execute-2).

data.Name: no-legacy-ssotme-json
data.Statement: Legacy ssotme.json files are retired in favor of effortless.json.
data.CheckMechanism: test ! -f <project>/ssotme.json
data.FixPlaybook: Merge entries into effortless.json and delete ssotme.json.

data.Name: rulebook-top-level-keys
data.Statement: Every rulebook has $schema, Name and Description top-level keys (no legacy model_name).
data.CheckMechanism: jq 'has("$schema") and has("Name") and has("Description")' <rulebook>
data.FixPlaybook: Add the keys; rename model_name to Name.

data.Name: transpiler-name-conventions
data.Statement: Transpiler Names are the squashed canonical form of the tool name with no typos.
data.CheckMechanism: Review Names against the tool catalog.
data.FixPlaybook: Re-register with effortless -install so the CLI writes the canonical Name.

data.Name: doctrine-matches-filesystem
data.Statement: CLAUDE.md and README doctrine cite only paths and projects that exist.
data.CheckMechanism: grep cited paths in CLAUDE.md against RulebookDomains.RelativePath.
data.FixPlaybook: Edit the doctrine file to the current layout.

data.Name: platform-rulebook-integrity
data.Statement: Every reference inside the platform rulebook resolves: FK values exist, catalog rows describe things that exist, formulas use the canonical dialect.
data.CheckMechanism: scratch validator (FK integrity + cycle + formula-dialect checks) run before every build; to be promoted into orchestration/.
data.FixPlaybook: Repoint or null the reference, record the reason in the field Description, and mark the finding fixed.

data.Name: transpiler-versions-live
data.Statement: Every transpiler a build depends on resolves to a live tool: no pins to decommissioned hosts, and every tool in the pipeline is published as [latest] on the tools server.
data.CheckMechanism: effortless build must reach every transpiler without Host-not-found retries; compare PinnedVersion/LastUrl in effortless.json against effortless listToolUrls.
data.FixPlaybook: Remove the stale pin (demos run rulebook-to-postgres at [latest]); publish the missing tool with scripts/publish-tool.sh; until then run it locally and effortless -setToolUrl to localhost.
data.SourceDoctrine: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md § Publishing an ssotme / effortless transpiler tool

data.Name: universal-start-contract
data.Statement: The root and every governed toy/example have one executable ./start.sh that fails loudly, cleanly restarts its intended experience, and prints declared localhost URLs.
data.CheckMechanism: ProjectSlotWitnesses records executable start.sh presence plus bash syntax, declared-port restart behavior, modeled URL declarations, and explicit health contracts.
data.FixPlaybook: Add or repair the project's explicit start.sh; do not probe legacy paths or substitute another project's experience.

data.Name: legacy-runner-retirement
data.Statement: The promoted root platform has no runtime dependency on the legacy portal or two-rulebook overlay, and every runner capability the platform still needs names its successor surface.
data.CheckMechanism: Inventory runner capabilities and search root runtime/config/documentation references; every match has a recorded promote, separate, replace, or retire decision.
data.FixPlaybook: Record the successor in LegacyRunnerCapabilities (root, standalone tool, generated or CLI surface) and point documentation at it. The runner keeps its copy; never delete runner files to satisfy this rule.

data.Name: canonical-project-shape
data.Statement: Every governed root, toy, and example fills the canonical slots required for its project kind, as witnessed from disk and effortless.json.
data.CheckMechanism: scripts/scan-project-slots.py refreshes ProjectSlotWitnesses; vw_rulebook_domains.required_gap_count must be zero.
data.FixPlaybook: Satisfy the missing explicit slot or correct the governing model; never substitute a legacy path or inferred success.

data.Name: init-db-fresh-database
data.Statement: A project's init-db step loads a newly created, empty database to completion; no step may require schema that a later step creates.
data.CheckMechanism: Create an empty database, run the project's init-db step against it, and require zero errors and a complete manifest.
data.FixPlaybook: Order validation that needs the live schema after the SQL that creates it, or make it create-if-missing; never rely on a previous load being present.
data.SourceDoctrine: CLAUDE.md § Avoid silent fallbacks; PLATFORM-EXPLORER-PLAN.md § Canonical consistency contract (init path)

data.Name: rulebook-write-path-minimal
data.Statement: Any tool that writes a rulebook JSON changes only the rows and fields it was asked to change; key order, formatting and derived values are untouched.
data.CheckMechanism: Edit one raw field through the write path, then git diff --stat the rulebook: the diff must touch only that row.
data.FixPlaybook: Write through a diff-minimal path (scripts/mark-finding-fixed.py, scripts/record-finding.py, json.dumps indent=2 of the loaded file) until the tool is fixed; never commit a rewrite produced by the offending tool.

data.Name: unbounded-external-probe
data.Statement: A build step must never make an unbounded call to an external daemon or network service. Any such call carries an explicit wall-clock bound and reports plainly when it steps over an unresponsive dependency.
data.CheckMechanism: Grep build-invoked scripts for docker/curl/ssh calls with no timeout wrapper. On macOS there is no timeout(1), so the bound must be written explicitly.
data.FixPlaybook: Wrap the call in a bounded helper that kills the child past N seconds and returns 124, then branch on that status with a message naming what was skipped.
data.SourceDoctrine: A hung probe inside a build is worse than a failed one: the work already succeeded, the CLI eventually kills the process, and a green result is reported as a failed build. Bound it, say so, move on.

data.Name: harness-metadata-shape
data.Statement: Code reading the conformance harness's _substrate_results.json must handle last_successful_run being present-but-null. The harness writes that key only when a substrate scored a full 100, so it is null for every substrate that has never been perfect.
data.CheckMechanism: Any '.get("last_successful_run", {})' is wrong -- the key exists, so the default never applies and the caller gets None. Use 'or {}' and branch explicitly.
data.FixPlaybook: Score from last_successful_run when it is truthy; otherwise take status and score from last_run and record the per-field counts as null rather than inventing them.
data.SourceDoctrine: A default that only fires on a MISSING key silently becomes None on a present-but-null one. Fail on the shape you actually get, not the shape you assumed.

data.Name: input-spoke-out-of-build
data.Statement: No reverse-sync INPUT spoke runs in a normal build pipeline. A spoke that writes into the rulebook is invoked deliberately, by a named script, never as a step every build walks.
data.CheckMechanism: Grep every effortless.json for a transpiler whose direction is substrate-to-rulebook (postgres-calculated-to-rulebook, airtable-to-rulebook) with IsDisabled false.
data.FixPlaybook: Set IsDisabled true and record why in the Description. Keep the deliberate invocation path (regenerate-answer-keys.sh calls the injector directly with ERB_WRITE_COMPUTED=true against a temp database).
data.SourceDoctrine: Rulebook JSON is HEAD. A build that writes to HEAD makes the hub a function of when and where it last ran, which is exactly what having a single source of truth is supposed to prevent.

data.Statement: A table's FK values reach Postgres exactly as the rulebook states them.
data.CheckMechanism: For every table with no intended <Entity>Id key that has a calculated Name, compare each row's Name to its slug (lowercase, non-alphanumerics collapsed to '-'). Any difference means rulebook-to-postgres will store a different value than the rulebook in the PK and in every FK that references it.
data.FixPlaybook: Give the table a leading raw <Entity>Id holding the key verbatim, so rulebook-to-postgres selects it as the PK instead of synthesizing one. Longer term rulebook-to-postgres should either keep the identity verbatim or refuse to rewrite FK text a formula reads.
data.SourceDoctrine: rulebook-to-postgres synthesizes <Table>Id = Slug(Name) for a table with no <Entity>Id and a calculated Name, and rewrites every referencing FK to that slug so FK == PK. Joins stay consistent, but any formula that renders the FK or compares it to the target's own text field silently computes against the slug; the build is green and the answers are wrong.

data.Name: domain-root x cr-15
data.Detail: The platform's own regression suite disappeared mid-session and only the corpus runner noticed. Commit 487f9782 'Restore the open-source transpilers to their pre-Talisman limits' (2026-09-09 16:29, another session, 7388 deletions) reverted orchestration/formula_parser.py by 247 lines and deleted all six orchestration/tests/test_formula_*.py files plus the testing/closure-golden fixtures. The suite had passed 92 tests at 16:10 in this same session. Restoring the test files is NOT the fix -- they assert the parser behaviour that commit deliberately removed, and fail 67/92 against the rolled-back parser. Whoever owns that rollback needs to say whether the suite should come back with it. TestSuites.TestFileCount now witnesses this so a registered pytest suite with nothing to run reads 'no-test-files' in the registry instead of only failing at run time.

data.Name: domain-ross-style-business-rules x cr-15
data.Detail: rulebook-to-postgres mistranslates a lookup wrapped in IFERROR. Claimants.PolicyIsActive is '=IFERROR(INDEX(Policies!{{IsActive}}, MATCH({{Policy}}, Policies!{{PolicyId}}, 0)), FALSE)'. The transpiler emitted it BOTH as a base-table column reference 't.policy_is_active' (which does not exist, so 03-create-views.sql fails with 'column t.policy_is_active does not exist' and the whole database reset aborts) AND as a mangled calc named calc_claimants_policy_is_active_policy_id. IFERROR is not in the documented dialect; the build stays green and only the db reset fails, so it hid until the corpus runner exercised the reset. Rulebook-side workaround is to drop the IFERROR wrapper, since INDEX/MATCH already yields NULL on no-match -- NOT applied here, because changing a demo's rulebook semantics is the owner's call. Add IFERROR to the CLAUDE.md formula-dialect trap list.

data.Name: domain-root x cr-15
data.Detail: scripts/run-corpus.py stamped FinishedOn and cleared its live flag as soon as the last project finished -- before it appended the CorpusRuns rows and before the root effortless build that projects them. Between those two points scripts/init-root-db.sh drops and recreates erb_effortless_rulebooks, so every corpus view is absent; a reader that treated 'all projects done' as 'run finished' queried them mid-reset and got 'relation vw_corpus_runs does not exist'. Hit while reading the 2026-09-09 third baseline. Fixed: status.json now carries an explicit phase (running | recording | building-root | done | root-build-failed) and finished_on is stamped only after the root build returns; the explorer's /corpus page shows the post-fan-out phases instead of reporting 'finished'.

data.Name: domain-root x cr-16
data.Detail: Nothing in any project is pinned (doctrine, 2026-09-09). The CLI writes LastUrl/LastVersionUsed after every build and RESOLVES TO LastUrl on the next one instead of re-resolving the bare tool name, making them a de-facto pin that rots. The corpus held 270 such keys across 39 manifests, 26 distinct pins, 10 pointing at decommissioned Control Plane workloads the CLI retries 10x6s before failing the build. The two fields also disagreed: 18 projects recorded LastVersionUsed v2026.08.30.1537 alongside a LastUrl for v2026-06-06-0219. All 270 stripped via scripts/unpin-transpilers.py. Because the CLI re-adds them on every build and offers no opt-out, erb_project.build_project() now strips them immediately before each build, so every build resolves [latest] and the pin written back is only ever a record of what [latest] was at that moment.

data.Name: domain-root x cr-20
data.Detail: The CLI's -exec takes only the FIRST token of its value and drops the rest, so '-exec bash reset-rulebook-db.sh' runs bare bash, which blocks on stdin until the CLI kills the build ('Timed out waiting for process to complete: bash'). Single-token '-exec ./script' is therefore the only working form in effortless.json -- which makes those steps depend on an executable bit that the CLI's own clean-and-recreate pass drops during the very build that then tries to run them. 6 of 38 projects failed this way in the 2026-09-09 baseline. Not fixable from this repo; needs a CLI fix. The corpus runner is immune because its own db phase invokes 'bash postgres-bootstrap/reset-rulebook-db.sh' directly.

data.Name: repo x cr-21
data.Detail: effortless-rulebook-editor POST /api/save-changes rewrites all 35 tables (rowsExported 1880) for a one-field row edit: 64,250 diff lines, keys reordered and every derived column (reverse relationships, aggregations, calcs) baked into data rows. Witnessed 2026-09-05 on cr-16-05 Status; reverted with git checkout. The root explorer therefore writes findings through scripts/mark-finding-fixed.py and only PATCHes the editor's base table for the live view.

data.Name: domain-root x cr-22
data.Detail: scripts/init-root-db.sh called 'docker info' unguarded to decide whether to nudge the generated editor container. With Docker Desktop unresponsive that call blocks forever; because it is the last step of the root build, every 'effortless build' at the repo root hung there until the CLI killed it with exit 255 -- a fully reset database reported as a failed build, which in turn blocked scripts/run-corpus.py's final recording step. Fixed 2026-09-09: every docker call in that script is now wall-clock bounded (run_bounded, 10s) and prints exactly what it skipped.

data.Name: domain-root x cr-23
data.Detail: scripts/run-conformance.py crashed with AttributeError on any project having a substrate that had never scored 100 -- which is most of the corpus. It went unnoticed because the single-project path had only ever been pointed at projects whose substrates were all green. Surfaced by the first corpus fan-out (toy-rulebooks/customer-fullname, xlsx at 50%). Fixed 2026-09-09 in build_rows().

data.Name: domain-star-trek x cr-24
data.Detail: postgres-calculated-to-rulebook was enabled in the build pipeline of 22 projects. It caused 18 of the 38 failures in the 2026-09-09 corpus baseline by failing on a missing .pg-raw-data.json. Adding the pull-from-postgres.sh step that produces that file does make the build pass -- and was rejected, because the spoke then rewrites RAW values despite its own Description claiming 'raws verified, never written': one star-trek build rewrote 1018 raw datetime values, round-tripping them through Postgres and baking the building machine's timezone into the hub (Ratings.CreatedAt '2026-01-12T19:46:59Z' -> '2026-01-12T13:46:59-06:00'). Disabled in all 22 on 2026-09-09; traffic-ticket-contest had already reached the same conclusion independently. The load-bearing use, postgres-bootstrap/regenerate-answer-keys.sh, is untouched.

RulebookTables had no <Entity>Id; Postgres stored 'witnessloops' where the rulebook says 'WitnessLoops'. RulebookTables.PolicyCount compared AccessPolicies.TargetTable (slug) to TableName (verbatim), so all 82 tables read IsUnsecured and all 194 RoleSchemaViews read IsDegenerateView (ColumnCount 0). Found on 2026-09-13 because the OWL substrate, which keeps the rulebook's text, disagreed on 674 answers. Fixed in model: RulebookTables.RulebookTableId (b9cbe25f); Postgres now reports 70 guarded / 12 unsecured tables and 0 degenerate views.

Claimants (5 rows) and Claims (5 rows) take the synthesized slug PK path: Postgres stores slugged keys and slugged FK text. No formula currently reads that FK text, so conformance is unaffected; any future formula that renders or compares those FKs will silently compute against the slug.
Users, Customers, Orders, Payments, JetModels, FlightControlSystems and OrderLines (45 rows) take the synthesized slug PK path; same exposure as ross-style-business-rules.

ProjectSlotWitnesses.Description: Strict filesystem/manifest witnesses for every governed project x canonical slot. Refresh with scripts/scan-project-slots.py.

schema.name: ProjectSlotWitnessId
schema.Description: PK: <domain>:<slot>.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Order 1. Display alias.

schema.name: Domain
schema.Description: FK to the governed project row.

schema.name: Slot
schema.Description: FK to the canonical layout slot.

schema.name: IsPresent
schema.Description: The strict scan currently passes this slot.

schema.name: WitnessedPath
schema.Description: The matched repository-relative path or transpiler Name.

schema.name: WitnessedDetail
schema.Description: Exact observed success or failure.

schema.name: WitnessedOn
schema.Description: ISO date of the scan.

schema.name: PresentFlag
schema.Description: Order 1. 1 when present.

schema.name: SlotRequiredForRoot
schema.Description: Order 1. Whether the slot is required of the repository root.

schema.name: SlotRequiredForExample
schema.Description: Order 1. Whether the slot is required for full example implementation.

schema.name: SlotRequiredForToy
schema.Description: Order 1. Whether the slot is universal for toys.

schema.name: DomainArea
schema.Description: Order 1. Physical project area.

schema.name: DomainKind
schema.Description: Order 1. The declared Kind (root | toy | example) of the witnessed project.

schema.name: DomainIsException
schema.Description: Order 1. Whether the row is a doctrine-sanctioned non-project container.

schema.name: IsRequiredHere
schema.Description: Order 2. The slot is required for this row's declared Kind.
schema.formula: =AND(NOT(COALESCE({{DomainIsException}}, FALSE())), OR(AND({{DomainKind}} = "root", COALESCE({{SlotRequiredForRoot}}, FALSE())), AND({{DomainKind}} = "example", COALESCE({{SlotRequiredForExample}}, FALSE())), AND({{DomainKind}} = "toy", COALESCE({{SlotRequiredForToy}}, FALSE()))))

schema.name: ImplementationGapFlag
schema.Description: Order 2. 1 when this absence prevents full implementation.
schema.formula: =IF(AND(NOT({{IsPresent}}), NOT(COALESCE({{DomainIsException}}, FALSE())), OR(AND({{DomainKind}} = "root", COALESCE({{SlotRequiredForRoot}}, FALSE())), AND({{DomainKind}} <> "root", COALESCE({{SlotRequiredForExample}}, FALSE())))), 1, 0)

schema.name: UniversalGapFlag
schema.Description: Order 2. 1 when a universal slot is absent.

schema.name: IsGap
schema.Description: Order 3. Required here and absent.

schema.name: GapFlag
schema.Description: Order 3. 1 when this required-here slot is absent.

schema.name: RequiredHereFlag
schema.Description: Order 3. 1 when this slot is required here.

schema.name: RequiredPresentFlag
schema.Description: Order 3. 1 when a required-here slot is present.

schema.name: WitnessState
schema.Description: Order 4. gap | filled | optional-empty.

schema.name: IsBlockingGap
schema.Description: Order 5. A current required-here conformance blocker.

data.Name: primary
data.Description: effortless-rulebook.json is the DURABLE SSoT. Input spokes (admin portal, Airtable, LLM, manual JSON) all write into it. Output spokes (Python, Go, Postgres, Excel, OWL, PlantUML, Explain-DAG, English, COBOL, ARM64, Entity Framework, Airtable reverse-sync) all read from it. Every substrate passes the same conformance tests.

__meta__.Description: Project-level metadata that travels with the rulebook: tagline, motif, narrative descriptions, substrate list, signature rows, etc. One row per metadata key. Use ValueType to interpret StringValue vs JsonValue.

schema.name: MetaKey
schema.Description: The metadata key (e.g. 'tagline', 'motif_palette', 'substrates'). Unique within the table.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Order 1. Identifier for this metadata entry. Mirrors MetaKey so the row is addressable by Name like every other table.

schema.name: ValueType
schema.Description: How to interpret the value columns: 'string' (use StringValue), 'object' (parse JsonValue as JSON object), 'array' (parse JsonValue as JSON array).

schema.name: StringValue
schema.Description: Plain string value. Populated when ValueType == 'string'; null otherwise.

schema.name: JsonValue
schema.Description: JSON-encoded value. Populated when ValueType == 'object' or 'array'; null when ValueType == 'string'.

data.StringValue: One repo, one shape: every Effortless project laid out the same way, graded by its own rulebook.

The repo-governing rulebook. Projects, the canonical shape, consistency rules and findings, the delivery programme, the skill catalog, and the mobile exploration plan — all as rows, all graded by derived fields.

2026-08-30: the platform became the repo. effortless-platform/ and the root-level runner machinery moved to rulebook-examples/legacy-runner/; the governing rulebook moved to ./effortless-rulebook/. 2026-09-07: the demotion was reversed. rulebook-examples/legacy-runner/ no longer exists; the orchestrator, ssotme-proxy, execution substrates, and conformance harness moved back to the repo root, and legacy-runner-rulebook.json was merged into this file. The admin portal was deleted outright, replaced permanently by the React explorer (./start.sh --portal). 2026-09-12: the effortless CLI absorbed the transpiler bus. ssotme-proxy/ was deleted; each injector is now a script tool under effortless-tools/ hosted by `effortless serve -port 4242`, and every project's step URL moved from localhost to 127.0.0.1.

schema.name: Name

schema.name: TestScript
schema.Description: Conformance test script: take-test.py

schema.name: TranspilerSource
schema.Description: licensed-effortless-tool | local-injector | external. WHO BUILT THE GENERATOR — provenance, not trustworthiness. Replaces the old IsProduction column. See FramingInvariants.framing-003.

schema.name: Maturity
schema.Description: prototype | demonstrating | reference-quality — how complete THIS substrate's implementation is. Independent of TranspilerSource.

schema.name: ExpressiveCompleteness
schema.Description: full | partial-aggregation | partial-formula | shape-only — which formula classes this substrate can faithfully evaluate. A factual property of the substrate engine.

schema.name: CanBeAnswerKey
schema.Description: Can serve as the oracle (SSoT) in a conformance run if the user designates it. True for any substrate whose output is fully witnessable. NOT an authority ranking — see ax-002.

schema.name: Determinism
schema.Description: deterministic | stochastic | externally-influenced — pure-function reproducibility class of the substrate

schema.name: RuntimeKind
schema.Description: database | spreadsheet | binary | text-emit | graph | docs — what kind of artifact this substrate produces / runs as

schema.name: Status
schema.Description: Operational status (active, proof-of-concept, deprecated). Lifecycle, not trustworthiness.

schema.Description: Purpose and capabilities

data.Name: Start → Admin Portal
data.Steps: User runs ./start.sh | Detect active rulebook project | Start the local transpiler host on :4242 if not running | Launch the CLI orchestrator menu (./start.sh --portal instead brings up the React explorer + generated rulebook editor)
data.Outputs: CLI orchestrator menu (or the React explorer with --portal), local transpiler host running

data.Name: Project Build (via the local transpiler host)
data.Steps: User triggers build in admin portal OR runs `effortless build` in active project | effortless CLI walks ProjectTranspilers in active project's effortless.json | For each transpiler with proxy URL, POST rulebook to localhost:4242 | Proxy invokes injector script | Generated files written to project's output folders
data.Triggers: Admin portal Build button, CLI `effortless build`, or post-save hook after rulebook edit
data.FlowLabel: Project Build (via the local transpiler host)

data.Name: Pull from Airtable (optional input spoke)
data.Steps: User chooses 'Pull from Airtable' in admin portal | Call airtable-to-rulebook | Write effortless-rulebook.json | Reload portal Postgres editor from JSON
data.Triggers: Admin portal action OR legacy CLI menu

data.Name: Admin Save (Write-Through Invariant)
data.Steps: Developer edits in portal | Backend writes to Postgres (live editor state) | SAME REQUEST writes to effortless-rulebook.json on disk | Backend returns success only if BOTH writes succeeded | Optional: trigger flow-002 (rebuild substrates)
data.Triggers: Any save action in admin portal (table edit, field edit, formula edit, sample data edit)
data.Outputs: Updated Postgres row, updated effortless-rulebook.json, optional substrate rebuild
data.Invariant: Postgres is the EDITOR; effortless-rulebook.json is the DURABLE SSoT. If Postgres is dropped, the rulebook reconstitutes it. If the JSON is dropped, the editor has no source of truth.

data.Name: Portal Bootstrap (auto-create DB + migrate)
data.Steps: Portal backend boots | Check if PG database 'erb_<domain>' exists | If missing, create it | Read effortless-rulebook.json | Run rulebook-to-portal-schema migration (creates tables for rulebook entities + AppUsers + AppRoles + AppNav) | Seed Postgres rows from rulebook JSON | Mark bootstrap complete
data.Triggers: First boot of admin portal for a project, OR explicit reset action
data.Outputs: Postgres database ready for editing, portal navigation populated

data.Name: Rehydrate Postgres from Rulebook JSON
data.Steps: User drops or corrupts Postgres | User runs ./start.sh or clicks Reset Editor | Backend re-runs flow-005 | Editor is back online from JSON SSoT
data.Triggers: Manual reset, DB loss, or version-control checkout to a different rulebook
data.Outputs: Postgres editor rebuilt to match rulebook JSON exactly

data.Name: Conformance Testing
data.Steps: Load test cases YAML | Run each substrate's take-test.py | Collect outputs | Compare results | Generate report | Display in admin portal Tests screen
data.Triggers: Admin portal 'Run Tests' button or CLI option V
data.Outputs: conformance-report.html, pass/fail matrix shown in portal

data.Name: Switch Active Project
data.Steps: User selects a different rulebook project in portal | Update orchestration/active-domain.txt | Reload portal pointing at new project's rulebook | flow-005 if Postgres for that project not yet bootstrapped
data.Triggers: Project switcher in admin portal nav
data.Outputs: Portal now editing the chosen project's rulebook + Postgres editor

data.Name: Clean Generated Files
data.Steps: User triggers Clean in portal Tech Tools OR CLI | Walks ProjectTranspilers | Each route invoked with clean=true | Generated outputs removed
data.Triggers: Tech Tools → Clean Build, or CLI option C

SubstrateContractPhases.Description: The three-phase contract every execution substrate implements. Inject is structural (schema → SDK), Execute is functional (compute), Grade is comparison. All three are 100% domain-agnostic — they translate whatever the rulebook defines without knowing what it means. Together with EvaluationSteps (the substeps within each phase) and EvaluationArtifacts (the JSON files that flow between phases), this forms the full evaluation subgraph: Phase → Steps → Artifacts.

schema.Description: Filename pattern under each execution-substrates/<technology>/ folder.

schema.name: WhyDomainAgnostic
schema.Description: Explains how this phase remains generic — i.e. what it must NOT contain.

schema.Description: FK to EvaluationArtifacts.ArtifactId — the canonical input artifact this phase consumes. [Soft reference to EvaluationArtifacts.ArtifactId; kept raw because EvaluationArtifacts.Produced/ConsumedByPhaseId already point artifacts -> phases and a FK here would create a table-level cycle.]

data.Name: Execute
data.Description: Reads blank-test.json, populates the generated entity structures, calls the generated Calc*() functions to fill in computed columns, emits test-answers.json.
data.WhyDomainAgnostic: The test runner does NOT know what fields mean. It just unmarshals JSON, calls the generated functions, and remarshal the result. Same main() pattern works for every rulebook.
data.FailureMode: take-test calls a hand-written helper instead of a generated Calc*() function — substrate now encodes business logic instead of just hosting it.

data.Name: Grade
data.Input: test-answers.json (substrate output) + answer-key.json (from rulebook seed data)
data.Description: Field-by-field, row-by-row comparison of every substrate's test-answers.json against the canonical answer-key.json derived from the rulebook seed data. No substrate holds a privileged position; answer keys come from the rulebook, not from any one substrate.
data.WhyDomainAgnostic: The grader compares JSON structures. It has no opinion about which fields exist or what they mean — disagreement is reported field-by-field.
data.FailureMode: Grader pre-decides which substrate is authoritative — that's a privileged-substrate bug (violates ax-002). Or it aggregates pass/fail without preserving the field-level diff.

data.Name: Inject
data.Output: Runnable substrate artifact (SDK / schema / workbook / ontology / DDL)
data.Description: Reads the rulebook schema and generates entity structures (1:1 with entities) plus computation functions (1:1 with computed columns). When the rulebook changes, re-running the injector regenerates the substrate artifact — the injector itself never changes.
data.WhyDomainAgnostic: The injector script must contain ZERO domain words (no 'language', 'workflow', 'syntax', 'customer'). It only translates generic rulebook structures into target-language constructs.
data.FailureMode: Injector mentions any domain word — that's the signature of a leak. The fix is in the injector, never in a hand-edit to the substrate output.

EvaluationSteps.Description: Substeps within each SubstrateContractPhase. Inject, Execute, and Grade each decompose into a small number of concrete substeps the orchestrator executes in order. This is the layer below SubstrateContractPhases — it answers 'what specifically happens inside phase-execute?' Used by the admin portal's Tests screen to render the actual stages a substrate run goes through.

data.Name: Load blank-test
data.Description: Read blank-test.json — rows with raw fields populated and all calculated fields nulled out.
data.Invariant: Blank-test is the SAME file for every substrate in a given run — substrates do not pre-process it.

data.Name: Hydrate entities
data.Description: Construct in-memory entity instances from the rows, using the substrate's generated structures.
data.Mechanism: Generated constructor / DDL insert / workbook row
data.Invariant: Hydration uses only generated code; no manual entity construction.

data.Name: Compute calculated fields
data.Description: Invoke each generated Calc<Field>() function to fill in calculated, lookup, and aggregation fields.
data.Invariant: Substrate executes generated functions only — it does NOT recompute formulas itself or inline business logic.

data.Name: Emit test-answers
data.Description: Serialize the fully-populated row set to test-answers.json.
data.Invariant: Output schema matches blank-test schema row-for-row, field-for-field.

data.Name: Load answer-key
data.Description: Read answer-key.json — the canonical expected values derived directly from the rulebook seed data (NOT from any one substrate's output).
data.Invariant: Answer key is rulebook-derived. If it comes from a substrate, you have a privileged-substrate bug.

data.Name: Collect substrate outputs
data.Description: Gather every substrate's test-answers.json from execution-substrates/<tech>/ output directories.
data.Invariant: All substrates are gathered as peers; none is treated as the reference.

data.Name: Compare field-by-field
data.Description: For each (row, field) pair, compare substrate value to answer-key value. For the English substrate, hand off to FuzzyGradingProviders for LLM-graded comparison.
data.Mechanism: Deep equality for deterministic substrates; orchestration/llm-fuzzy-grader.py for English.
data.Invariant: Disagreement is reported at the field level, not as a binary pass/fail per substrate.

data.Name: Emit report
data.Description: Write per-substrate test-results.md and aggregate all-tests-results.md; render orchestration-report.html for the portal Tests screen.
data.Invariant: Report preserves field-level disagreement; aggregate pass-rates never erase the diff.

data.Name: Load rulebook JSON
data.Description: Read effortless-rulebook.json from disk (or from EFFORTLESS_INPUT_DIR via the local transpiler host). Validate that it parses and has a schema block per table.
data.Invariant: No domain knowledge encoded in the loader — it parses generic JSON.

data.Name: Walk entities
data.Description: Iterate every top-level table in the rulebook; for each, emit one entity structure in the target language (class, struct, table, OWL class, etc.).
data.Invariant: Emission is purely structural — entity name and field names come from the rulebook, never hardcoded.

data.Name: Compile formulas
data.Description: For every calculated/lookup/aggregation field, transpile its formula expression into a target-language function (Calc<Field>).
data.Invariant: Compiler honors the rulebook's declared FormulaDialect; substrate-specific extensions are an error, not a feature.

data.Name: Write substrate artifact
data.Description: Persist the generated code/schema/workbook under execution-substrates/<technology>/ or licensed-effortless-tools/<technology>/.
data.Mechanism: Filesystem write; never an in-memory-only artifact.
data.Invariant: Artifact is reproducible: same rulebook + same injector version = byte-equivalent output (modulo deterministic ordering).

EvaluationArtifacts.Description: The JSON / Markdown files that flow between SubstrateContractPhases. Each artifact is a contract: a file with a known schema produced by one phase and consumed by the next. This table is the artifact registry — what each file IS, where it lives, who writes it, who reads it. Together with SubstrateContractPhases.InputArtifactId/OutputArtifactId, this gives the evaluation pipeline a fully-witnessed data-flow graph.

schema.name: Format
schema.Description: json | markdown | html | binary | source-tree

schema.name: PathPattern
schema.Description: Where the artifact lives on disk, with <placeholders> for variable parts.

schema.name: ProducedByPhaseId
schema.Description: FK to SubstrateContractPhases.PhaseId — the phase that writes this artifact. Null for inputs that come from outside the evaluation pipeline (e.g. the rulebook itself).

schema.name: ConsumedByPhaseId
schema.Description: FK to SubstrateContractPhases.PhaseId — the phase that reads this artifact. Null for terminal outputs (e.g. the human-facing report).

schema.name: DerivedFrom
schema.Description: Plain-text description of how this artifact is derived — important for proving no substrate is privileged.

schema.name: IsSourceArtifact
schema.Description: Order 1. Not produced by any phase (an input to the contract).

schema.name: IsJson
schema.Description: Order 1. Artifact format is JSON.

schema.name: ProducerPhaseName
schema.Description: Order 1. Producing phase name.

schema.name: ConsumerPhaseName
schema.Description: Order 1. Consuming phase name.

schema.name: ProducerStepCount
schema.Description: Order 2. Steps in the producing phase.

schema.name: IsJsonSource
schema.Description: Order 2. A JSON input to the contract.

schema.name: ProducerIsProductive
schema.Description: Order 3. Whether the producing phase is productive.

schema.name: IsPipelineHandoff
schema.Description: Order 3. Produced by a decomposed phase and passed onward.

schema.name: ArtifactRole
schema.Description: Order 4. seed / handoff / terminal.

schema.name: IsSeedArtifact
schema.Description: Order 5. JSON input that seeds the contract.

data.Name: answer-key.json
data.DerivedFrom: Rulebook seed data — every field including computed ones, evaluated FROM THE RULEBOOK (not from any substrate). The canonical oracle.
data.Description: The grader's reference. Rulebook-derived so no substrate is privileged. If you find yourself sourcing answer-key from one substrate's output, that's a bug (violates ax-002).

data.Name: blank-test.json
data.DerivedFrom: Rulebook seed data with all calculated/lookup/aggregation fields nulled out. Produced by orchestration, not by any substrate.
data.Description: The exam: rows with raw fields populated and computed fields blank. Every substrate gets the SAME blank-test for a given run.

data.Name: Rulebook JSON
data.DerivedFrom: Hand-authored OR pulled from Airtable via airtable-to-rulebook (an input spoke, not a phase output).
data.Description: The single durable SSoT for a project. All other artifacts in this table are mechanically derivable from this one.

data.Name: Substrate artifact
data.Description: A runnable artifact in the target technology — Python module, Go package, Postgres DDL, OWL ontology, Excel workbook, ARM64 binary, etc.

data.Name: test-answers.json
data.Description: A substrate's exam answers — the same rows as blank-test, with computed fields filled in by THAT substrate.

data.Name: test-results.md / all-tests-results.md
data.DerivedFrom: Field-level diff of every substrate's test-answers.json against answer-key.json.
data.Description: Human-readable grade report. Aggregated by orchestration/generate-report.py into orchestration-report.html for the portal Tests screen.

SubstrateTradeoffDimensions.Description: The fixed taxonomy of dimensions used to characterize every substrate. Pro/con statements in SubstrateTradeoffs are scoped to one of these dimensions, so substrates can be compared apples-to-apples (e.g. 'who's fastest?' = filter SubstrateTradeoffs by DimensionId=dim-speed). Adding a dimension here means committing to fill it in for every substrate.

schema.name: Order
schema.Description: Display order in UI.

schema.name: Tradeoffs
schema.Description: Reverse relationship: SubstrateTradeoffs rows whose DimensionId points here.

schema.name: TradeoffCount
schema.Description: Order 1. Tradeoff rows on this dimension.

schema.name: HasTradeoffs
schema.Description: Order 2. At least one substrate is assessed on this dimension.

schema.name: FullyExpressiveTradeoffCount
schema.Description: Order 3. Tradeoffs on this dimension from fully expressive substrates.

schema.name: FullCoveragePercent
schema.Description: Order 4. Percent of tradeoffs on this dimension from fully expressive substrates.

schema.name: IsFullyCovered
schema.Description: Order 5. Only fully expressive substrates are assessed here.

data.Name: Accuracy
data.Description: Observed conformance rate on the answer-key — deterministic substrates are 100% by construction; stochastic substrates are bounded by their grading model.
data.Tradeoffs: tr-binary-accuracy, tr-csv-accuracy, tr-dag-accuracy, tr-ef-accuracy, tr-go-accuracy, tr-owl-accuracy, tr-pg-accuracy, tr-python-accuracy, tr-uml-accuracy, tr-xlsx-accuracy

data.Name: Debuggability
data.Description: How easy it is to investigate a failure: stepping through generated code, inspecting intermediate state, reading the artifact in a familiar tool.
data.Tradeoffs: tr-binary-debug, tr-csv-debug, tr-dag-debug, tr-ef-debug, tr-go-debug, tr-owl-debug, tr-pg-debug, tr-python-debug, tr-uml-debug, tr-xlsx-debug

data.Name: Expressive completeness
data.Description: Which formula classes the substrate can faithfully evaluate: full | partial-aggregation | partial-formula | shape-only.
data.Tradeoffs: tr-binary-expr, tr-csv-expr, tr-dag-expr, tr-ef-expr, tr-go-expr, tr-owl-expr, tr-pg-expr, tr-python-expr, tr-uml-expr, tr-xlsx-expr

data.Name: Portability
data.Description: How easily the substrate artifact moves to a different host environment — copy a file, ship a binary, require a database server, require an LLM API key.
data.Tradeoffs: tr-binary-port, tr-csv-port, tr-dag-port, tr-ef-port, tr-go-port, tr-owl-port, tr-pg-port, tr-python-port, tr-uml-port, tr-xlsx-port

data.Name: Provenance
data.Description: Who built the generator — licensed-effortless-tool | local-injector | external. Distinct from quality; see FramingInvariants.framing-003.
data.Tradeoffs: tr-binary-prov, tr-csv-prov, tr-dag-prov, tr-ef-prov, tr-go-prov, tr-owl-prov, tr-pg-prov, tr-python-prov, tr-uml-prov, tr-xlsx-prov

data.Name: Runtime cost
data.Description: Money cost per run. Deterministic substrates are effectively zero; LLM-graded substrates cost API tokens.
data.Tradeoffs: tr-binary-cost, tr-csv-cost, tr-dag-cost, tr-ef-cost, tr-go-cost, tr-owl-cost, tr-pg-cost, tr-python-cost, tr-uml-cost, tr-xlsx-cost

data.Name: Speed
data.Description: How fast a single conformance run completes for this substrate. Spans <1s to multi-minute.
data.Tradeoffs: tr-binary-speed, tr-csv-speed, tr-dag-speed, tr-ef-speed, tr-go-speed, tr-owl-speed, tr-pg-speed, tr-python-speed, tr-uml-speed, tr-xlsx-speed

data.Name: Witnessability
data.Description: Whether the substrate's output is structured enough to serve as an answer-key oracle in a conformance run. See ExecutionSubstrates.CanBeAnswerKey.
data.Tradeoffs: tr-binary-witness, tr-csv-witness, tr-dag-witness, tr-ef-witness, tr-go-witness, tr-owl-witness, tr-pg-witness, tr-python-witness, tr-uml-witness, tr-xlsx-witness

The same fixed dimension set (see SubstrateTradeoffDimensions) is applied to every substrate, so 'why pick Postgres over Python?' or 'why does English cost so much?' is answerable by filtering this table. NOT a ranking — see ax-002 (no privileged substrate). Each row records a factual property along one comparable axis.

data.Name: substrate-001:dim-accuracy
data.Pro: Deterministic — same input always produces same output.
data.Con: Partial-formula coverage means it fails conformance on formula classes it doesn't yet handle.

data.Name: substrate-001:dim-runtime-cost
data.Pro: Effectively free per run.

data.Name: substrate-001:dim-debuggability
data.Con: Stepping through ARM64 assembly is impractical for business-rule debugging.

data.Name: substrate-001:dim-expressive-completeness
data.Con: partial-formula — many higher-level formula constructs are not yet emitted.
data.Note: Demonstrates the floor: a binary substrate is possible at all, not that it's complete.

data.Name: substrate-001:dim-portability
data.Pro: Single binary file — copy and run on any ARM64 host.
data.Con: Architecture-locked: an x86 box needs a re-compile or emulator.

data.Name: substrate-001:dim-provenance
data.Pro: Local injector — fully open and inspectable.

data.Name: substrate-001:dim-speed

data.Con: Inject + assemble + link adds compile-time overhead; not interactive.
data.Note: Proof-of-concept; speed has not been benchmarked head-to-head with Python/Go.

data.Name: substrate-001:dim-witnessability
data.Con: Cannot serve as answer-key — binary output is not structurally inspectable as JSON.

FuzzyGradingProviders.Description: LLM providers usable for fuzzy grading of the English substrate — the ONLY non-deterministic substrate. All other substrates execute formulas deterministically; English requires an LLM to interpret prose into computed values. Use low temperature (0.1) for repeatability.

Tools the developer can install into the active project via the Add Tool screen. Same catalog the `effortless -install` CLI consumes; the portal is just a thin UI over the CLI so behaviour stays canonical.
The architectural pattern that makes the platform work: input spokes write to the rulebook, output spokes read from it, conformance binds them.
The cold-start story: from `git clone` to a running portal with a default user landing on Home.
Delivery phases of the repo-consistency programme. Contract table for rulebook-to-progress-report. QuotedPrice values are illustrative planning weights, not invoices.

The effortless.json contract that both the admin portal and the CLI consume. There is ONE pipeline definition per project; both surfaces are thin wrappers around `effortless build` so they stay in lockstep.
One-line CMCC framing for the platform rulebook itself: what it is, what it generates, and what conformance it claims.

The catalog of Claude Code skills that make up the effortless-skills skill set (repo renamed from effortless-claude). Each skill is a loadable instruction set that pre-teaches Claude everything it needs to work in an ERB project — naming conventions, pipeline mechanics, formula semantics, etc. Skills are the answer to the LLM learning-curve problem: instead of every user teaching Claude from scratch, the learning is encoded once and loaded on demand. LocalMirrorPath is a derived artifact: clone-skills.sh pulls a live copy of each skill from the source repo so the docs/skills/ mirror stays current.

One row per substrate graded within a ConformanceRuns run. Mirrors the per-substrate entries of testing/_substrate_results.json (last_run + last_successful_run.test_results) written by orchestration/test-orchestrator.py.

One row per invocation of the cross-substrate conformance harness (orchestration/test-orchestrator.py) against a governed project. Imported by scripts/run-conformance.py from that project's testing/_substrate_results.json.
Witnessed violations of ConsistencyRules, one row per (domain, rule) occurrence. This is the sweep work queue.
Repo-wide consistency invariants as data. Each row is a checkable rule with a fix playbook; ConsistencyFindings rows are its violations.
End-to-end flows from rulebook to execution and testing

One row per (corpus run x project). Carries the per-phase outcome — build, database reset, conformance — so a red project is red for a NAMED phase instead of a grepped log line, and links to the ConformanceRuns row it produced.
One row per corpus-wide fan-out (scripts/run-corpus.py). Append-only history: how much of the corpus was green on a given day is read straight off these rows.
Delivery disciplines splitting programme effort. Client-visible SharePercent must sum to 100 (progress-report hard requirement).

Curated narratives that demonstrate ERB capabilities in motion: substrates 'follow along' as the rulebook changes. Two narrative styles coexist: (1) commit-sequence narratives (legacy) where a single demo rulebook evolves over commits; (2) cross-rulebook narratives (current) where the same demo is observed across DIFFERENT rulebooks side-by-side. Cross-rulebook supersedes commit-sequence because RulebookDomains now form a tree (ParentDomainId) — the progression is data, not git history.
External tools and their roles
The intended developer path through the portal: Home → project → Rulebook → Substrates → Builds → Tests → Input Spokes → Users.
What is being committed to for a story, one testable statement per row. The unit of pricing and the acceptance ledger.
The phases work is scheduled and priced in. Exactly one phase is the current bid.

The identity facts a row filter may refer to as {{name}}. Each becomes a generated helper function app.name() that reads the current transaction token or resolves from other helpers. Seeded with user_id, email and role.
How every quoted price divides across kinds of work. The client-visible shares must sum to 100.
Complexity bands a story is placed in. The weight multiplies acceptance criteria into units of work, so it moves the price. The most demanding band must be named G3.
The large themes user stories are grouped under. Each epic belongs to one package.
Feature categories (epics) of the programme (progress-report contract).
Individual features of the programme (progress-report contract).
One row per field of every table in this rulebook, mirrored by the Sync step. Field-level permissions point at these rows.
Capability packages of the platform programme (progress-report contract).
Your own prose for the Progress Report, keyed by section. A meta table that drives the document only.
A per-field override for one role, used to hide or protect individual columns such as cost, margin or personal data that the table-level grant would otherwise expose.
A per-table override of one role default CRUD and row filter. A table with no row here inherits the role defaults.

A named role that users hold. Its default CRUD and default row filter apply to every table unless an ERBRoleTablePermissions row overrides them. Each role becomes a database role and gets its own schema of permitted views.
One row per table in this rulebook, mirrored from its structure by the Sync step. Security permissions and delivery features point at these rows rather than at bare table names.
The atom of scope: one selectable piece of work, placed in a phase, an epic, a feature and an effort class.
The people and service accounts that sign in to the application, each holding one role. Identity helpers can resolve a signed-in user to a row here by email or external id.
Effort/complexity classes for user stories (progress-report contract; the most demanding class must be literally named G3).

The JSON / Markdown files that flow between SubstrateContractPhases. Each artifact is a contract: a file with a known schema produced by one phase and consumed by the next. This table is the artifact registry — what each file IS, where it lives, who writes it, who reads it. Together with SubstrateContractPhases.InputArtifactId/OutputArtifactId, this gives the evaluation pipeline a fully-witnessed data-flow graph.

Substeps within each SubstrateContractPhase. Inject, Execute, and Grade each decompose into a small number of concrete substeps the orchestrator executes in order. This is the layer below SubstrateContractPhases — it answers 'what specifically happens inside phase-execute?' Used by the admin portal's Tests screen to render the actual stages a substrate run goes through.
Runtime environments that execute business rules derived from the rulebook

Names every field-type the rulebook supports, with intent and example formula shape. Lets the UI explain what makes a calculated field different from a lookup field from an aggregation, instead of just showing a type tag.

Junction table linking RulebookFlavors to RulebookTags (many-to-many via junction). A flavor can have any number of tags; a tag can apply to any number of flavors. The portal renders each flavor's tags as colored chip rows in the grid and uses them to drive the filter panel.

Catalog of formula dialects that a rulebook can declare. Per-rulebook formula dialect is headline feature #6: each demo rulebook names which dialect it speaks (in _meta.formulaDialect), and substrates honor that declaration. The platform rulebook does not enumerate which functions a dialect supports — that lives in each demo rulebook's own formula definitions. This catalog only registers the dialects themselves.

Mistakes-to-avoid catalog. Each row is one wrong framing that has been caught and corrected, paired with the right framing and the axiom it violates. The portal surfaces these so future agents (and humans) can be re-grounded without rediscovering them.

LLM providers usable for fuzzy grading of the English substrate — the ONLY non-deterministic substrate. All other substrates execute formulas deterministically; English requires an LLM to interpret prose into computed values. Use low temperature (0.1) for repeatability.

Authoritative glossary for the ERB platform. Every term used in orchestration code, docs, the admin portal UI, or rulebook tables appears here EXACTLY ONCE, with a definition AND an ImplementedAs pointer back into this rulebook (or to source files when the implementation is code rather than data). If a term appears in repo prose but has no row here, that's a documentation bug. If a term has a row here but no ImplementedAs target, that's an architecture bug — every concept should be data, code, or a value.

Succession ledger for the legacy-runner promotion and its 2026-09-07 reversal. legacy-runner/ was a transitional staging area (2026-08-30 to 2026-09-07) for the root platform infrastructure (orchestrator, transpiler bus, execution substrates, conformance harness); it no longer exists as a directory, and that infrastructure is root infrastructure again. Each row records the capability, the original promote/separate/replace/retire decision, and — where the decision was reversed — an honest new decision and rationale. The admin portal capability was retired outright (deleted, not restored); every other reversed row is restored to root.

Primary navigation groups of the root explorer (app/). Rendered as a top navigation bar at desktop width and a bottom tab bar at phone width; each group roots a MobileRoutes subtree. The table name is historical: there is no separate /m mobile shell.

Route surface of the root explorer (PLATFORM-EXPLORER-PLAN.md §3): deep-linkable routes under each navigation group. Screen names the React component (pages/<File>.jsx:<Export> under app/src/) that implements the route and stays blank until it exists, so the derived unbuilt counts are the Phase 3 build backlog.
Positive-form invariants the project is built on. These are the load-bearing claims; if any one is dropped, the methodology no longer holds. FramingInvariants are mistakes that violate these axioms.
Central orchestration logic that coordinates rulebook loading, injection, and testing

The catalog of distinctive features the ERB platform offers. The rulebook is the formal SSoT for this list; the repo's README and per-feature README files MUST conform to these rows. Each feature has a one-line summary (the elevator pitch), a Tier (headline vs additional), a Priority (sort order within tier), and a ReadmeFilePath (where the long-form explanation lives — even if it's still a stub). IsReadmeStub is calculated so 'which READMEs are still missing' is a queryable fact, not a tribal one. Many features reference an OntologyAxiom — that's the axiom the feature operationalizes.
The portal and the `./start.sh --cli` interface are peer interfaces to the same effortless.json pipeline; portal behaviour cannot drift from CLI behaviour.
Configuration files and their purposes
The primary goal of the platform: the load-bearing claim the project is built to demonstrate.
One explicit launch contract for every governed project or intentional container.
The canonical root/example/toy project shape as first-class, scan-witnessed data.
Explicit localhost services and health endpoints owned by project launch profiles.
Project overview
Strict filesystem/manifest witnesses for every governed project x canonical slot. Refresh with scripts/scan-project-slots.py.
The resilience claim: dropping the Postgres editor at any time is safe, because `./start.sh` rebuilds it from JSON.

Customer ontologies: each domain has its own rulebook + substrate generation. Domains form a TREE — ParentDomainId links a more-elaborate domain back to the simpler one it grew out of (e.g. Talisman ADVANCED ← Talisman BASIC). The UI uses this to present related rulebooks as a set rather than a flat list, and to drive 'next step in the progression' navigation.

Classification of each demo rulebook under rulebook-examples/. Lets the UI group projects by what they're TEACHING — a tutorial ladder is a different beast from a computation-heavy ontology. Density numbers come from a static analysis of each rulebook (calculated/aggregation/lookup counts).
Peer input spokes that can write into effortless-rulebook.json. The rulebook JSON is the durable SSoT; these are interchangeable sources.

Tag catalog for RulebookFlavors. Each tag has a color and emoji so it renders as a visible chip in the portal. Tags are flexible attributes — a flavor can have many tags. Browse/filter the flavors grid by any combination of tags.
Directed edges of the skill meta-conversation: which skill routes to which, and why (orchestrator routing table + see-also cross-references).
Local HTTP transpiler server on localhost:4242. Each transpiler is an HTTP route; injectors are the route bodies. Used by `effortless build` to call substrate generators uniformly.

The three-phase contract every execution substrate implements. Inject is structural (schema → SDK), Execute is functional (compute), Grade is comparison. All three are 100% domain-agnostic — they translate whatever the rulebook defines without knowing what it means. Together with EvaluationSteps (the substeps within each phase) and EvaluationArtifacts (the JSON files that flow between phases), this forms the full evaluation subgraph: Phase → Steps → Artifacts.

The fixed taxonomy of dimensions used to characterize every substrate. Pro/con statements in SubstrateTradeoffs are scoped to one of these dimensions, so substrates can be compared apples-to-apples (e.g. 'who's fastest?' = filter SubstrateTradeoffs by DimensionId=dim-speed). Adding a dimension here means committing to fill it in for every substrate.

Per-(Substrate × Dimension) Pro/Con/Note. The same fixed dimension set (see SubstrateTradeoffDimensions) is applied to every substrate, so 'why pick Postgres over Python?' or 'why does English cost so much?' is answerable by filtering this table. NOT a ranking — see ax-002 (no privileged substrate). Each row records a factual property along one comparable axis.

Registered test suites. One DECLARED row per suite the corpus runner is expected to execute: the repo-root formula-parser pytest suite plus one cross-substrate conformance suite per governed project. IsRegistered is a declaration, never inferred from the filesystem; the AnswerKeyCount / HasEffortlessJson / HasPostgresBootstrap columns are witnessed by scripts/scan-test-suites.py so RegistrationState can say WHY a registered suite is not yet runnable.
Conformance testing: prove all substrates compute identically
User stories of the repo-consistency programme (progress-report contract).
The portal-vs-rulebook write-through invariant: Postgres is the live editor, JSON is the durable SSoT, every save writes to both.
